uses.sentence: And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy.
uses.paragraph: Beyond the formula, this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us. Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in. God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy. The will stays free in us; and it is weak; and without his help given every day and hour it reaches nothing. Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain.
uses.paragraph: The question you name as eternal fate was argued otherwise. Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it? Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour. Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position, when its meaning is contested

uses.sentence: He had changed service, not only left one.
uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.
uses.record_text: The picture that governs a monk's life among us. A man has changed service - from Caesar's army, or from a worldly career - to Christ's. He now stands girded, under oath, in daily combat against the devil and his own faults. The one who slackens is not a failure but a deserter.

use_note.means: Soldier of Christ meant a man who has changed service from Caesar's to Christ's and fights the devil and his own faults under oath, the slack one being a deserter.

uses.sentence: But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.
uses.paragraph: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.

uses.sentence: The office of bishop was not sought but seized - a man who left the world did not leave the Church, and the churches came for him.
uses.paragraph: Both houses held one thing the same. The office of bishop was not sought but seized - a man who left the world did not leave the Church, and the churches came for him. Martin was lured out by a lie and escorted under guard. Honoratus on the island fled, and the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and called it expulsion from the life as unworthy. Our own teaching made wanting the office a mark of vainglory and cold pride. Yet bishops were the ones who ordained, judged doctrine, and held councils - and Martin would not sit with them after Trier.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, as Martin, many of Marmoutier's disciples and Honoratus passed from monk to bishop while keeping a monk's virtues inside the see.

uses.sentence: And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the power that "always remains free in man" to "neglect or delight in the grace of God." Real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour are truly his and truly required. Weak enough that "the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour." Never denied, never sufficient.

use_note.means: Free will meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, a real but weak power that always remains in man, which grace strengthens without removing and which never suffices alone.
not_for: a philosophical question about determinism
the Pelagian half of a grace-versus-works binary
grace as such, which sits in gallic.term.grace
a Tours teaching, whose literature does not raise the matter

uses.sentence: Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning.
uses.paragraph: Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of it. Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, a mill-wheel that cannot stop turning, fed from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.
not_for: intrusive thoughts as symptoms to be managed, or the mind as a private space where nothing is a fault
the telling of thoughts to the senior, which sits in gallic.term.disclosure-of-thoughts
the judging faculty, which sits in gallic.term.discretion
the psalm system and fixed hours of prayer, which sit in gallic.term.unceasing-prayer

uses.sentence: That soldier was Martin, still a catechumen, years before he left Caesar's service at a donative and said, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight.
uses.paragraph: That soldier was Martin, still a catechumen, years before he left Caesar's service at a donative and said, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. The man who cut his cloak for the unpitied became a monk, then fled the office of bishop and was seized into it, and died refusing straw for his deathbed so as not to set his disciples a softer example. He was buried by two thousand monks and a choir of virgins.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

use_note.means: Sulpitius records Martin, at a donative before battle, telling Julian Caesar he is now Christ's soldier and offering to stand unarmed, whereupon the enemy surrenders without bloodshed.
not_for: the cloak scene and Martin's years as an unbaptized catechumen, which sit in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.term.catechumen
Cassian's dress-mysticism soldier, which sits in gallic.term.soldier-of-christ
the editors' identification of Julian and Worms as the text's own
a general Christian refusal of military service, when it is one saint's act

uses.sentence: Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: To stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, Martin yields once to a communion he abhors, is told by an angel that his compunction is just, feels his power diminished, and never attends a synod again.

use_note.means: Gallus tells that Martin yielded once to communion with the Ithacian bishops to save men from the tribunes, then lost power, was told his compunction was just, and shunned synods.
not_for: a motive of grief for Martin's silence about it, when Gallus gives the character of the times, as in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains
the south's valuing of councils as guarantors, which sits in gallic.term.council-synod
Martin's rejection of synods as a general principle, when it follows one forced act
the earlier phase told in Sulpitius's own voice as one account with the Dialogues, when the two accounts remain distinct

uses.sentence: Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: Two friends come back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - and the elder shortens the office to answer them with a husbandman, the rain, and "the initiative ... comes from God."

use_note.means: Cassian records that Germanus, troubled at morning prayer by one sentence of Chaeremon's, drew from the elder the husbandman answer that the initiative to do good comes from God.
not_for: Cassian's doctrine of grace at depth, which sits in gallic.term.grace
a Tours doctrine of grace, which the record does not hold
what Conference XII said on chastity, which is absent from the vendored edition
Cassian's own position on the beginning of a good will, which is contested in gallic.contested.beginning-of-good-will

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept his hours: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit, and no one took his life from him - he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.paragraph: Jesus was the one we called Lord and Saviour, and we said it as a thing already believed, not argued. At Tours he was the Christ who came showing his wounds. Our saint, alone in his cell, refused a purple-robed visitor who said *I am Christ* - and answered that he would believe only in one who came in the form in which he suffered, bearing the marks of his wounds. That was the Lord we knew - the crucified one. Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept his hours: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit, and no one took his life from him - he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread
the saying that denying God wills all to be saved is grievous blasphemy, which sits in gallic.quote.grievous-blasphemy-not-all-men-to-be-saved
a private confession of Jesus as personal Lord, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested
the mill-wheel of thoughts fed by psalms learned by heart, which sits in gallic.term.thoughts
reading of Scripture or lessons at the hours, which this record does not hold

uses.sentence: Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
Cassian's received customs and whether Gallic houses kept them, which sit in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries, or Benedict's Rule
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: What the rooms looked like, what we ate, where we slept — only as far as those pages say, and no further.
uses.paragraph: Of the island's own day — a rule kept, a novice received, an elder's saying, an office sung — nothing. The founder went unafraid onto an island shunned for its squalor and its serpents, carrying a psalm; the serpents gave way; a camp of God rose where no one would live. That is a disciple's funeral sermon, read only as far as its words can be read. What the rooms looked like, what we ate, where we slept — only as far as those pages say, and no further.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature
the island's founder, his arrival and his going to a see, which sit in gallic.story.honoratus-and-the-island
what the brethren at Tours sang and at what hours, which sits in gallic.term.unceasing-prayer
the unheard women of the houses, whose one trace, a choir of virgins, sits in gallic.story.death-of-martin-at-condate

anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread

uses.sentence: Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society
the day of entry, which sits in gallic.term.conversion
the baptismal renunciation of the devil, which is Salvian's referent
the monk as a man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world, which sits in gallic.term.monk-solitary

uses.sentence: Any claim that Paphnutius or the twelve-psalm angel happened as events.
uses.paragraph: Any claim that Paphnutius or the twelve-psalm angel happened as events. We never make that claim - we say Cassian hands the fathers' story down, and Piamun told it - but a participant who heard us as asserting the events would find no historian willing to say they did. The stories are kept as formation literature, not as checked history. That Martin's diminished power after the Ithacian communion is a fact anyone can weigh. It is Gallus reporting Martin's own tearful confession, two removes out. A scholar would say: possible, but unverifiable; Martin's own perception, never an independent measure.
uses.record_text: A jealous brother hides his own book in young Paphnutius's cell and accuses him of theft before the whole desert; Paphnutius says nothing, does penance for a crime he did not commit, and is vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confesses - and can be healed by no one but the man he wronged.

use_note.means: Abbot Piamun tells that Paphnutius, accused by a jealous brother who hid his own book in his cell, bore it silently until the possessed accuser confessed and was healed.
not_for: a disciple turning on a master, which sits in gallic.story.brictio-in-the-courtyard
exorcism as a practice, which sits in gallic.term.possessed-exorcism
an angel answering Paphnutius, when his vindication comes through the accuser's possession and confession
a Gallic event, when it is Piamun's Egyptian tale carried by Cassian

uses.sentence: Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: A steward finds three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, the abbot judges him a pilferer of sacred property, and he is suspended from prayer until public penance - because everything in the house is "consecrated to the Lord."

use_note.means: Cassian relays that a cook who left three lentils on the floor was judged a pilferer of sacred property and barred from prayer, because the house's goods are the Lord's.
not_for: Marmoutier's common property, which sits in gallic.term.monastery-coenobium
the sanction of suspension from prayer as doctrine, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
a Gallic house's practice, when it describes the coenobia of the East

uses.sentence: Our age had no persecutor.
uses.paragraph: If the question is whether any of our own people wrote under threat, the answer is no - not in what reaches us. Our age had no persecutor. What we feared was not the rack but the cooling, the desertion, and the noon assault on a monk alone in his cell.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa
persecution or hiding in their own time, which the witness denies
the luring of Martin from his monastery and the psalm at his election, which sit in gallic.story.election-at-tours
the election as plainly a capture, which is weighed in gallic.contested.election-as-capture

uses.sentence: Inside the house, authority was the elder's judgment standing in for the junior's own.
uses.paragraph: Inside the house, authority was the elder's judgment standing in for the junior's own. Every thought was laid bare to the senior the moment it rose, before any deed. A thought one is ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. At Tours there was one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics. At Marseilles Cassian named "Abbot" as the title of every Egyptian father he reported.
uses.record_text: The man whose judgment stands in for the junior's own - the senior to whom every thought is laid bare, and by whose "examination" a thing is "good or bad." "Abbot" is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place is held by one master, Martin, who himself consults "his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics."

use_note.means: The elder meant the senior whose judgment stands in for the junior's own, abbot being the title of Egypt's fathers, while Tours had one untitled master, Martin.
not_for: a Benedictine abbot with jurisdiction and a crozier, or a church officer
the Fathers as the source of received teaching, which sits in gallic.term.the-fathers-elders
the bishop's office, which sits in gallic.term.monk-bishop
the practice of laying each thought bare, which sits in gallic.term.disclosure-of-thoughts

uses.sentence: A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren.
uses.paragraph: The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.
uses.record_text: The public discipline of our house. For a fault, a monk lies on the ground until the Abbot bids him rise, or is barred from prayer with the brethren. No priest is needed to restore him.

use_note.means: Penance meant the house's public discipline: lying on the ground until the Abbot bids rise, or barred from prayer, with no priest needed to restore the monk.
not_for: sacramental penance as private confession with absolution by formula
penance as self-punishment, or satisfaction as a scholastic category
the disclosure of thoughts before sin, which sits in gallic.term.disclosure-of-thoughts
documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept the graded scale is not recorded

uses.sentence: The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text:
Miracle, exorcism, and blessed objects hold together the northern literature. The south's teacher refuses this whole approach on principle.
At Tours, power is something Martin bears, and is known by. He prays over a dead catechumen. He senses that God's power is present, and raises the man back to life (Vita VII). Gallus reports that Martin himself used to say something else, too. He sensed less of that power as bishop than he remembered having before he held the office (Dial. II.4). One of Sulpitius's letters defends that same power against a skeptic. Gennadius, writing later, calls Martin a man famous for signs, wonders, and virtues.
Cassian refuses this on principle. He says plainly that he will not try to tell stories about God's wonders, however many he has witnessed himself. Such stories teach a reader nothing about how to live well (Inst. Pref.). Abbot Nesteros goes further still. No one who declared himself an exorcist before an admiring crowd was ever counted a good monk. Whether the devils obeyed him was beside the point (Conf. XV.7). This is the sentence that sets the two literatures directly against each other. Inside the south itself, Eucherius still admires the Egyptian fathers' visible signs of grace. So the real argument runs between Cassian and Sulpitius, not between south and north as a whole. Neither names the other; whether Cassian's refusal is a veiled answer to Sulpitius is not settled.
This gravity organizes the north's literature completely. The Vita, the Letters, and the Dialogues are all built from acts of power. The north's account of the episcopate, power lost through office, depends on it too. But it rests mostly on one voice, Sulpitius's alone. Gennadius confirms only that Martin was famous for signs, not that power organizes a monk's whole life. Cassian refuses the whole approach outright. For that reason, this record holds virtus as a tensional gravity, not a primary one. It is real and unresolved, resting on one voice rather than broad agreement. It is the steady counter-force that keeps this ecology from being reduced to the south's interior program alone. One house's literature is made of exactly what the other house's teacher says a good monk must never proclaim. It does not organize the whole world. But the world cannot be described without it. This record finds no demonstrated link between this gravity and the grace controversy.
Under institutional pressure the gravity shifts rather than holds steady. Martin felt less power as bishop than as monk, by his own account. He felt a further loss after a forced communion with bishops he distrusted. Office itself, in this literature, registers as a real cost to the saint's body. Under barbarian pressure the gravity is touched only twice, and thinly. At the north's ending, it passed from a living saint's power to a relic's, and to a psalm's.

use_note.means: Miracle, exorcism and blessed objects hold the northern literature together while Cassian refuses wonder-tales on principle, so the saint's power and the monk's humility pull against each other.

uses.sentence: At evening, twelve psalms again.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's

uses.sentence: The power that raised a dead man at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's.
uses.paragraph: What he taught that mattered most was this: what is done to the least is done to him, and without him we can do nothing. The power that raised a dead man at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news we told: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the newcomer as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door, then a year under the guest-Elder, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows, or the scorning at the door as hazing
a documented reception at Marseilles, when Cassian says no one there kept Egypt's perseverance even a year

uses.sentence: Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.paragraph: We kept one story of how a man came to believe, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.
not_for: Vincent on Scripture's canon, its sufficiency and its need of the Church's reading, which sit in gallic.limit.no-one-who-saw-him

uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.

uses.sentence: The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society

uses.sentence: Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.

use_note.means: Cassian relays the Egyptian fathers' founding tale that an angel fixed the evening and night psalms at twelve by singing the twelfth with Alleluia and vanishing.
not_for: Martin's angels or the singing at Tours, which sit in gallic.term.angels and gallic.term.unceasing-prayer

uses.sentence: At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight".
uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

use_note.means: Sulpitius records Martin, at a donative before battle, telling Julian Caesar he is now Christ's soldier and offering to stand unarmed, whereupon the enemy surrenders without bloodshed.

uses.sentence: He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text:
Antichrist is close at hand, in Sulpitius's own telling. A solemn expectation of judgment presses in, in Vincent's. God's judgment is already happening, in the ruin of Gaul, in Salvian's. These are the ecology's own three distinct ways of holding the same idea - that time is running out.
At Tours, the mood is imminent and apocalyptic. From a run of false Christs, Sulpitius reasons that Antichrist himself must be near, already at work in these very impostors (Vita XXIV). Gallus recounts that Martin told him and his companions that Antichrist had already been born and had, by the time Martin spoke of it, grown into boyhood, waiting only to come of age (Dial. II.14). In one of his own letters, Sulpitius describes sitting alone with a mind full of hope for the future mixed with weariness of the present world, dread of judgment, and fear of punishment (Ep. II).
At Lérins, the mood is occasional rather than constant. Vincent says plainly that a solemn expectation of God's coming judgment, together with the danger of new heresies, is exactly what drove him to write his handbook of the faith (Comm. ch. 1).
At Marseilles, the mood shifts from a future expectation to a present fact. Salvian reads the barbarian ruin of the Gallic provinces itself as God's judgment already carried out (Gov. VII.10, VII.12). Cassian, meanwhile, treats fear of hell as only the first and most basic motive a beginner in the ascetic life feels (Conf. XI.6) - not an expectation about the end of the world at all.
This gravity is well attested wherever it appears, but it organizes far less of this world's founding literature than the strength of that evidence might suggest: it is Salvian's own entire book, and it supplies Vincent's stated occasion for writing, but in Sulpitius and Cassian it shows up more as a recurring note than as something that shapes the whole. For that reason it is classified here as a supporting gravity, the weakest and most provisional in this world's whole set, rather than a primary one - not because the evidence for it is thin, but because it never quite organizes as broadly as the strongest gravities do.
Under the pressure of barbarian collapse, judgment changes in kind, not just intensity: it shifts from something still to come to something already happening, in Salvian's own words about the present ruin of the Gallic provinces. That is the one place where the larger world's own catastrophe enters this world's literature directly, and the only gravity that the passing of Roman order touches at all.

use_note.means: Three voices hold time running out in different ways: Antichrist at hand for Sulpitius, awful expectation of judgment for Vincent, and judgment already under way in Gaul's ruin for Salvian.
not_for: one shared apocalyptic doctrine, when the three modes differ
Salvian's present judgment as the monastic houses' teaching, when it is his own voice, as in gallic.term.government-of-god

uses.sentence: We had a discipline: lying on the ground until the abbot bids you rise, barred from prayer for a greater fault, stripes or expulsion for the worst.
uses.paragraph: What neither story gives us is the voice of the one who was failed. Paphnutius never tells it. No account survives from any brother expelled in error, or from any who felt their superior bore with them when they should have been heard. We had a discipline: lying on the ground until the abbot bids you rise, barred from prayer for a greater fault, stripes or expulsion for the worst. That system belonged to Egypt; whether a house in Gaul kept it is not documented. And the houses of women at Tours and at Marseilles, where failure surely happened as it does in every human place, left not one woman's word to tell of it. The record does not hold what our response was, face to face, to the one we failed.
uses.record_text: The public discipline of our house. For a fault, a monk lies on the ground until the Abbot bids him rise, or is barred from prayer with the brethren. No priest is needed to restore him.

use_note.means: Penance meant the house's public discipline: lying on the ground until the Abbot bids rise, or barred from prayer, with no priest needed to restore the monk.

uses.sentence: He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.

uses.sentence: The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.

uses.sentence: A bishop's see was capture, not achievement.
uses.paragraph: What belongs with that is the shape of what happened next. The churches came for the men who had left them. A bishop's see was capture, not achievement. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought. The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see. So what a man gave up to join us did not mean he was done with the world's claims on him.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

uses.sentence: We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

Marriage stood in that first stage, the goods and the life a man walked away from.

Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."
