uses.sentence: At Tours our record does not give the day hour by hour.
uses.paragraph: At Tours our record does not give the day hour by hour. What it gives is the saint in his cell - a wooden hut, rarely leaving it except for prayer, keeping his mind on prayer even at other work the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The aim was the same; the system is not told.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

That debt belonged to us. We said it could not be paid without him. But whether that debt is carried from birth, or comes only with a person's own willing and acting, our record does not say. uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

uses.sentence: We owe unhesitating loyalty not to what a few people made up, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian held the same grammar. We owe unhesitating loyalty not to what a few people made up, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement. At Tours Martin would not honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity to warrant it. Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent quoted it: let nothing new be brought in - nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

uses.sentence: So yes - we held there was no other way to say it.
uses.paragraph: Jesus is God. We said it as a thing already believed, not a thing we debated among ourselves. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So yes - we held there was no other way to say it.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.

uses.sentence: Martin, alone in his cell, saw a Christ in purple and told him he would believe only in one who showed the wounds.
uses.paragraph: And one private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, saw a Christ in purple and told him he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.
not_for: Vincent on Scripture's canon, its sufficiency and its need of the Church's reading, which sit in gallic.limit.no-one-who-saw-him

uses.sentence: Some bishops said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting.
uses.paragraph: The office fled and overtaken - that is the shape we lived. A man left the world for the stricter service of Christ, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, and a guard. Martin could not easily be drawn from his monastery, so a citizen threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. A bystander seized the psalter and read praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. Then the new bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa
persecution or hiding in their own time, which the witness denies
the luring of Martin from his monastery and the psalm at his election, which sit in gallic.story.election-at-tours
the election as plainly a capture, which is weighed in gallic.contested.election-as-capture

uses.sentence: A man left the world for the stricter service of Christ, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish.
uses.paragraph: The office fled and overtaken - that is the shape we lived. A man left the world for the stricter service of Christ, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, and a guard. Martin could not easily be drawn from his monastery, so a citizen threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Then the new bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant the man himself, cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.

uses.sentence: Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising.
uses.paragraph: Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of it. Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, a mill-wheel that cannot stop turning, fed from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.
not_for: intrusive thoughts as symptoms to be managed, or the mind as a private space where nothing is a fault

uses.sentence: A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the newcomer as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door, then a year under the guest-Elder, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows, or the scorning at the door as hazing
a documented reception at Marseilles, when Cassian says no one there kept Egypt's perseverance even a year
a forced turning to the monastic life, such as the murderer Moses of Calamus, which sits in gallic.term.conversion
a Tours grade, where disciples appear but no probationary rank, which sits in gallic.term.disciple-master

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested
the mill-wheel of thoughts fed by psalms learned by heart, which sits in gallic.term.thoughts
reading of Scripture or lessons at the hours, which this record does not hold

uses.sentence: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society

the baptismal renunciation of the devil, which is Salvian's referent
the monk as a man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world, which sits in gallic.term.monk-solitary

uses.sentence: A young monk named Paphnutius was accused of theft by a jealous brother before the whole desert.
uses.paragraph: A young monk named Paphnutius was accused of theft by a jealous brother before the whole desert. The accuser had hidden his own book in the young man's cell. Paphnutius said nothing in his own defence. He asked for a rule of repentance, did public penance for a crime he had not committed, and was vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged. That is Egypt's story, brought to us by Cassian. Whether any brother among us in Gaul stood wrongly accused, and whether he was believed, no one wrote down.
uses.record_text: A jealous brother hides his own book in young Paphnutius's cell and accuses him of theft before the whole desert; Paphnutius says nothing, does penance for a crime he did not commit, and is vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confesses - and can be healed by no one but the man he wronged.

use_note.means: Abbot Piamun tells that Paphnutius, accused by a jealous brother who hid his own book in his cell, bore it silently until the possessed accuser confessed and was healed.
not_for: a disciple turning on a master, which sits in gallic.story.brictio-in-the-courtyard

uses.sentence: One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood storms into the courtyard. He calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then repents within the hour. Martin will not remove him, saying he bears with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas.

use_note.means: Gallus relates that Brictio, raised by Martin, stormed at him and called his visions ridiculous fancies, repented within the hour, and was borne with as Christ bore Judas.
not_for: a neutral report of Brictio's case, when it comes from men hostile to him

uses.sentence: A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.
uses.paragraph: And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.

uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus reports that Martin refused to remove Brictio from the presbyterate when he was accused of crimes, lest he seem to avenge himself, saying Christ bore with Judas.

uses.sentence: Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
Cassian's received customs and whether Gallic houses kept them, which sit in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries, or Benedict's Rule
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity

uses.sentence: The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle.
uses.paragraph: Perfection cannot be gained without a monk's labours, and by those labours alone, without the grace of God, no one can attain it. At the moment a brother feels his fast has done something, he is taught to say *not I, but the grace of God with me*. Both halves are commanded. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position, when its meaning is contested
the night's scruple that prompted the question, which sits in gallic.quote.germanus-troubled-after-the-nights-teaching
Germanus's objection as Chaeremon's own view

uses.sentence: Every thought was laid bare to the senior the moment it rose, before any deed.
uses.paragraph: Inside the house, authority was the elder's judgment standing in for the junior's own. Every thought was laid bare to the senior the moment it rose, before any deed. A thought one is ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. At Tours there was one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics. At Marseilles Cassian named "Abbot" as the title of every Egyptian father he reported.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution, or therapy
public penance for a committed fault, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
the virtue that regulates all others on the royal road, which sits in gallic.term.discretion
a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: Then labour in his cell until evening.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

use_note.means: The cell meant the monk's own dwelling, at Tours a hut or cave rarely left except for prayer, at Marseilles a discipline holding the wandering heart still by labour.
not_for: a prison cell, or a bare private bedroom with solitude as privacy
the house as a whole, which sits in gallic.term.monastery-coenobium
the noonday hatred of the cell itself, which sits in gallic.term.accidie
Cassian's rule of never leaving the cell as proven Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is not documented

uses.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body.
uses.paragraph: We read to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The purpose was not learning but living. The fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So the psalms keep the mill fed with what is good. The immediate goal of the whole life is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every practice is ranked by whether it serves that mark.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
the cloak vision or the raised catechumen as evidence that the Lord rose, when they show the saint's power, as in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.raising-of-the-catechumen
the content of Cassian's seven books against Nestorius, which is unread
a chain of witnesses, when the world's floor stands more than three centuries after the events

uses.sentence: The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the newcomer as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door, then a year under the guest-Elder, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows, or the scorning at the door as hazing
a documented reception at Marseilles, when Cassian says no one there kept Egypt's perseverance even a year
a forced turning to the monastic life, such as the murderer Moses of Calamus, which sits in gallic.term.conversion
a Tours grade, where disciples appear but no probationary rank, which sits in gallic.term.disciple-master

uses.sentence: At the hours we kept what Cassian handed us from Egypt: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid.
uses.paragraph: Jesus was the crucified one who met us in the poor, and the Lord whose grace drew us while we were still unwilling. We held him as God - Vincent's formula from the island: in God one substance but three Persons, in Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh. At the hours we kept what Cassian handed us from Egypt: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.
uses.paragraph: What belongs with that is the shape of what happened next. The churches came for the men who had left them. A bishop's see was capture, not achievement. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought. The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see. So what a man gave up to join us did not mean he was done with the world's claims on him.
uses.record_text: An Egyptian bishop was "carried off from the assembly of anchorites." He tells two Gallic travellers that his office was an expulsion from the monastic life, and calls himself unworthy of it. He takes up his staff and leads them past himself, to the old men whose mere sight is a lesson.

use_note.means: Cassian reports meeting Archebius, an Egyptian bishop taken from the anchorites, who called his consecration an expulsion from monastic life and sent the travellers to the old men.
not_for: an independent witness to Archebius, when none survives outside Cassian
Gallic bishops as such, which sit in gallic.story.election-at-tours

uses.sentence: Nothing a man made up bound anyone.
uses.paragraph: Scripture stood first. Tradition and the fathers' consent stood with it, as the guard against every man reading it his own way. We were keepers, not authors. Nothing a man made up bound anyone.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty, stated by Cassian for custom, Vincent for doctrine and Martin for cult, though none cites another.
not_for: growth of doctrine without alteration, which sits in gallic.term.progress-vs-alteration
the test as consistently applied, when that is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
the novice's year under the guest-elder and the admission that none kept Egypt's perseverance a year, which sit in gallic.term.junior-novice
Scripture's sufficient canon and its need of the Church's reading, which sit in gallic.limit.no-one-who-saw-him

uses.sentence: Cassian said himself that no one in our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year.
uses.paragraph: No. Our span closed in the middle of the fifth century, and no church today is the same house we were then. What became of the brethren at Tours after Martin's death, and of the island after Vincent wrote, our record does not follow - that belongs to the centuries past our own close, and we speak from inside our years, never looking back on them the way a historian would. The Rule of Benedict, a century later, lies outside our window. The later cult and basilica of Martin's own city, the mid-470s synods that carried our argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks - all of that is not ours. What we can say is this. The customs we received from Egypt were kept in Gaul as far as the cold allowed, and admitted to be kept badly. Cassian said himself that no one in our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. So even in our own day we were not Egypt, and we knew it. Whether any house after us kept what we tried to keep, or how far what we held passed into the monasticism that came after, our record does not tell. We were two households in Gaul, between a soldier's discharge and the years after Ephesus. That is the life we can witness to, and its end is our own horizon.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant the whole body of Egyptian practice Cassian carried to a Gallic bishop's new house, received from the fathers, not his own Rule.
not_for: a codified Rule such as Benedict's, or the Institutes as a theology textbook
Vincent's rule of faith, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule
the content of one custom, such as the psalm system in gallic.term.unceasing-prayer or the dress in gallic.term.the-monks-dress
documented Gallic practice, when Cassian admits no one in our monasteries kept Egypt's perseverance unbroken even for a year

uses.sentence: Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. The trouble was not soldiers hunting believers. It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile the barbarians were pouring into the two parts of Gaul. Julian Caesar gathered an army at the city of the Vaugiones and began to hand out a bonus payment to the soldiers. As was the custom, they were called forward one by one, until it came to Martin's turn. Then he judged it a good moment to ask for his discharge. He did not think it right to take the payment if he was not going to stay in the service. So he said to Caesar: "Up to now I have served you as a soldier. Now let me become a soldier for God. Let the man who is going to serve you take your payment. I am the soldier of Christ. I am not permitted to fight."

use_note.means: Sulpitius narrates Martin refusing Julian's donative and asking discharge with the words 'I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.'
not_for: a refusal of pay on grounds of money, when the passage turns on a change of service
the offer to stand unarmed and the enemy's surrender, which sit in gallic.quote.martin-offers-to-stand-unarmed
a verbatim record of the exchange rather than Sulpitius's report of it
a rule binding every Christian soldier of the time

uses.sentence: The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
Cassian's received customs and whether Gallic houses kept them, which sit in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries, or Benedict's Rule
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

use_note.means: Egypt stands as the measure of real monastic life, received in the south as a rule from the fathers and matched at Tours by a saint said to outdo it.

uses.sentence: The third was renouncing "of what we have been" - that is, leaving behind the whole visible world itself and keeping the image of the world to come always in our mind.
uses.paragraph: Renunciation of the world was what made a monk. It had three stages in the fathers' teaching. The first stage, the easiest, was leaving "of what is not our own" - goods, gold, possessions - and that alone was not enough to confer perfection on the man who renounced. The second stage was renouncing "of what we are," which is the habits, vices and passions of soul and body that formerly ruled us. The third was renouncing "of what we have been" - that is, leaving behind the whole visible world itself and keeping the image of the world to come always in our mind. Marriage stood in that first stage, the goods and the life a man walked away from.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. uses.sentence: Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.

uses.sentence: What the power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer showed us is this: it was Christ's power, not the saint's.
uses.paragraph: What the power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer showed us is this: it was Christ's power, not the saint's. The grace of God always works together with our will; it goes before the will, helps it, and crowns it. Without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian set under every virtue a monk felt he had gained. And he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still.
uses.paragraph: Yes - a mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on.
uses.record_text: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. uses.sentence: He tells only that they watched Martin and were formed by him.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the way in was different. Martin began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who turned to Christ against his parents' wish and stayed unbaptized for years. He was baptized only after the night he saw Christ wearing half the cloak he had given to a beggar. uses.sentence: When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*.
uses.paragraph: And he was the one without whom we can do nothing. When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The office fled and overtaken - that is the shape we lived.
uses.paragraph: The office fled and overtaken - that is the shape we lived. A man left the world for the stricter service of Christ, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, and a guard. Martin could not easily be drawn from his monastery, so a citizen threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. A bystander seized the psalter and read praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. Then the new bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, as Martin, many of Marmoutier's disciples and Honoratus passed from monk to bishop while keeping a monk's virtues inside the see.

uses.sentence: From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.
not_for: a settled verdict that the teaching is semi-Pelagian, when that label is contested
