uses.sentence: And one elder is kept who confessed a power lessened.
uses.paragraph: And one elder is kept who confessed a power lessened. Martin took one communion he abhors, to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics, and afterward he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by it. But that is not the house answering to someone it failed; it is the saint's own judgment on himself.
uses.record_text:
Miracle, exorcism, and blessed objects hold together the northern literature. The south's teacher refuses this whole approach on principle.
At Tours, power is something Martin bears, and is known by. He prays over a dead catechumen. He senses that God's power is present, and raises the man back to life (Vita VII). Gallus reports that Martin himself used to say something else, too. He sensed less of that power as bishop than he remembered having before he held the office (Dial. II.4). One of Sulpitius's letters defends that same power against a skeptic. Gennadius, writing later, calls Martin a man famous for signs, wonders, and virtues.
Cassian refuses this on principle. He says plainly that he will not try to tell stories about God's wonders, however many he has witnessed himself. Such stories teach a reader nothing about how to live well (Inst. Pref.). Abbot Nesteros goes further still. No one who declared himself an exorcist before an admiring crowd was ever counted a good monk. Whether the devils obeyed him was beside the point (Conf. XV.7). This is the sentence that sets the two literatures directly against each other. Inside the south itself, Eucherius still admires the Egyptian fathers' visible signs of grace. So the real argument runs between Cassian and Sulpitius, not between south and north as a whole. Neither names the other; whether Cassian's refusal is a veiled answer to Sulpitius is not settled.
This gravity organizes the north's literature completely. The Vita, the Letters, and the Dialogues are all built from acts of power. The north's account of the episcopate, power lost through office, depends on it too. But it rests mostly on one voice, Sulpitius's alone. Gennadius confirms only that Martin was famous for signs, not that power organizes a monk's whole life. Cassian refuses the whole approach outright. For that reason, this record holds virtus as a tensional gravity, not a primary one. It is real and unresolved, resting on one voice rather than broad agreement. It is the steady counter-force that keeps this ecology from being reduced to the south's interior program alone. One house's literature is made of exactly what the other house's teacher says a good monk must never proclaim. It does not organize the whole world. But the world cannot be described without it. This record finds no demonstrated link between this gravity and the grace controversy.
Under institutional pressure the gravity shifts rather than holds steady. Martin felt less power as bishop than as monk, by his own account. He felt a further loss after a forced communion with bishops he distrusted. Office itself, in this literature, registers as a real cost to the saint's body. Under barbarian pressure the gravity is touched only twice, and thinly. At the north's ending, it passed from a living saint's power to a relic's, and to a psalm's.

use_note.means: Miracle, exorcism and blessed objects hold the northern literature together while Cassian refuses wonder-tales on principle, so the saint's power and the monk's humility pull against each other.

uses.sentence: The question of how what we kept connects to the earliest followers turns on a distinction we held as binding: received, not invented.
uses.paragraph: The question of how what we kept connects to the earliest followers turns on a distinction we held as binding: received, not invented. What matters is not the age of a practice measured in years but whose it is - handed down from the fathers, or made up by us. Among the brethren at Marseilles the whole program was received from Egypt's elders as the fathers' own. The twelve psalms at evening and at night came, Cassian says, from the fathers of Egypt in the days when only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the offices should hold fifty or sixty psalms. The Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the founding story as Cassian carried it to us - not our own invention but Egypt's witness to itself. Egypt was our measure, in the south received as the fathers' own rule.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

use_note.means: Novelty and antiquity named the axis on which all three founding voices judged legitimacy: the new is suspect for being new, and what was handed down is held fast.
not_for: novelty as harmless newness or as a virtue

uses.sentence: We met him in the poor - the beggar at the gate, the stranger at the door.
uses.paragraph: And the Lord we knew in our own life was the crucified one. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple who came without wounds. The Christ Martin would believe was the one who showed the marks of his suffering. We met him in the poor - the beggar at the gate, the stranger at the door. An elder of Egypt broke his fast for guests because, receiving Christ in them, he ought to refresh him.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.

uses.sentence: It required him to do what the elder said, to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose, and to let the elder's judgment stand in for his own.
uses.paragraph: There was space for obedience before certainty. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the virtue the fathers of Egypt put before all others - before reading, before silence, before even humility - was obedience. A junior learned it first by orders contrary to his liking, the conquest of his own wishes. That teaching never required a man to say he was certain. It required him to do what the elder said, to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose, and to let the elder's judgment stand in for his own. The fathers knew a man's own judgment could not be trusted alone - they called discretion the royal road between excess and slackness, where extremes meet. So a brother struggling with doubt would have been taught to bring the doubt to the elder, not to resolve it by himself.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

use_note.means: Discretion meant, for Cassian, the virtue Antony's council made mother and regulator of all others, the royal road between excess and slackness, where extremes meet.
not_for: tact, prudence or confidentiality, or a private intuition

uses.sentence: Whether any house in Gaul scorned a newcomer at the door for ten days, or searched him for a coin, or lodged him a year under the guest-elder, our record does not hold.
uses.paragraph: That is Egypt's door. What a house in Gaul did with a man who came to its own threshold, Cassian never wrote. He says only that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance a year. Whether any house in Gaul scorned a newcomer at the door for ten days, or searched him for a coin, or lodged him a year under the guest-elder, our record does not hold.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.

uses.sentence: Every thought was laid bare to the senior.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.

uses.sentence: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods.
uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.

uses.sentence: That Martin's diminished power after the Ithacian communion is a fact anyone can weigh.
uses.paragraph: Any claim that Paphnutius or the twelve-psalm angel happened as events. We never make that claim - we say Cassian hands the fathers' story down, and Piamun told it - but a participant who heard us as asserting the events would find no historian willing to say they did. The stories are kept as formation literature, not as checked history. That Martin's diminished power after the Ithacian communion is a fact anyone can weigh. It is Gallus reporting Martin's own tearful confession, two removes out. A scholar would say: possible, but unverifiable; Martin's own perception, never an independent measure.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

uses.sentence: At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the sixth fault, "which we may term weariness or distress of heart," "especially trying to solitaries." It makes the monk gaze at the sun "as if it was too slow in setting," and dresses his escape as pious duty until "the soldier of Christ becomes a runaway from His service, and a deserter."

At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.

He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. uses.sentence: Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.
uses.paragraph: Who settled it? Nobody, when it touched the hardest places. Hear the shape our own record gives it. Vincent, on the island, gave a test: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated. He looked to the decrees of councils - legitimate because they innovate nothing - as guards of the faith. That is the theory. What our record shows is a fracture that ran past it.

uses.sentence: From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: For us obedience is the virtue the Egyptians "put not merely before manual labour and reading and silence and quietness in the cell, but even before all virtues." It is proved by absurd and terrible commands - a dry stick watered for a year, a son carried to the river - and it is the first thing a junior learns, "to conquer his own wishes." At Tours it is what Sulpitius feels before Martin: "unlawful to do anything but acquiesce."

use_note.means: Obedience meant the virtue Egypt's fathers put before all others, proved by hard commands and learned first by the junior as conquering his own wishes.

uses.sentence: The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

use_note.means: Human effort and free choice are held real while grace goes before and crowns them, argued under Augustine's pressure as a relation Cassian says reason cannot fully grasp.

uses.sentence: What we are told is that Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.paragraph: At Tours our record dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap - not on what the brethren sang, or at what hours. What we are told is that Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.

uses.sentence: Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.

uses.sentence: We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.paragraph: Beyond the formula, this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us. Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in. God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy. The will stays free in us; and it is weak; and without his help given every day and hour it reaches nothing. Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help going before, working with and crowning the will, held on purpose with a free will in a relation beyond reason's grasp.
not_for: a binary of grace alone against works, or semi-Pelagian as a settled verdict, a label contested in gallic.contested.massilian-label

uses.sentence: What was handed down from antiquity is held fast.
uses.paragraph: We never agreed that anyone settled it. Our whole grammar ran the other way. The faith believed everywhere, always, by all is kept by holding to the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher - be he bishop, be he confessor, be he martyr. Vincent, on the island, wrote that test down against his own forgetting: when a part dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty appears, hold fast to antiquity; when a few stand against many, prefer the decree of an ancient council or, failing that, the collated writings of the fathers. Not one man's judgment, not one see's, but the consent of those who came before us. What is new - a doctrine, a custom, a cult - is suspect for being new. What was handed down from antiquity is held fast.
uses.record_text: For us tradition is what has been received from predecessors and must be passed on unchanged. Vincent's second criterion of truth after Scripture, "the Tradition of the Catholic Church." Pope Stephen's rule, "nothing but what has been handed down." Cassian's "traditions of the Elders" by which thoughts are judged. And the "steady tradition ... from antiquity" without which Martin will not honour a tomb.

use_note.means: Tradition meant what has been received and must be passed on unchanged, the ground on which Vincent's rule, Cassian's elders and Martin's refusal of a tomb are all judged.
not_for: a rival authority to Scripture in a confessional debate

uses.sentence: Jesus was the crucified one who met us in the poor, and the Lord whose grace drew us while we were still unwilling.
uses.paragraph: Jesus was the crucified one who met us in the poor, and the Lord whose grace drew us while we were still unwilling. We held him as God - Vincent's formula from the island: in God one substance but three Persons, in Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh. At the hours we kept what Cassian handed us from Egypt: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught the same: an elder broke his fast for strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.
uses.paragraph: At Tours our one private word comes from Martin alone in his cell. The devil came dressed in purple with a crown of jewels and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. And he was the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate; Martin, still a catechumen and a soldier, cut his one cloak in two, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught the same: an elder broke his fast for strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

uses.sentence: What we kept instead was this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: The question names a struggle - cannot manage to believe - and asks what we would say. Here is what our record lets us answer. We did not keep an argument for the unbeliever. No one among us wrote down a proof of the resurrection for someone who doubts it. What we kept instead was this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. At Tours Martin was ten when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is our one formation story, and it is one man's. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that grace kindles the first desire, not the will itself. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. And we held it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all to be saved. So what we would say is not that you must manage it, but that the calling comes first and the willing follows. We never told anyone they had to argue themselves into faith. We kept the catechumen a long time, watched what grace did, and counted the beginning of every good thought as God's. Beyond that our record does not reach - we have no treatise for the doubter, only the witness that grace draws the unwilling.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: Then the new bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.paragraph: The office fled and overtaken - that is the shape we lived. A man left the world for the stricter service of Christ, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, and a guard. Martin could not easily be drawn from his monastery, so a citizen threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. A bystander seized the psalter and read praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. Then the new bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, as Martin, many of Marmoutier's disciples and Honoratus passed from monk to bishop while keeping a monk's virtues inside the see.

uses.sentence: The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society

uses.sentence: Martin himself said that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding blood - in hunger, watchings, nakedness, and fasting.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin himself said that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding blood - in hunger, watchings, nakedness, and fasting. What Martin kept hidden was not himself but one story - the affair at Treves and the communion he yielded to, which he hid because of the times. He kept it from everyone but us, not because hiding was necessary for survival but because he never forgave himself the price. The secrecy was his own grief, not a general danger. Our record holds no catacombs, no underground gatherings, no flight from soldiers. What it holds instead is a monk who left Caesar's service and gathered brethren openly across the river from a city, and houses at Marseilles that sent their trained men to fill the churches' sees. If you are asking about another people's hiding in another age, that is not our own.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa

uses.sentence: From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - the whole southern formation program: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing without the vocabulary - Martin's discernment of Anatolius's robe and of the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV) - but 'no "purity of heart," no "discretion," no fault-list.' Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. Two of Cassian's own conferences on this program, on chastity and on nocturnal illusions, and one book of the Institutes, do not survive in the English edition this account draws on.

use_note.means: Purity of heart as goal, discretion as regulator and the eight faults as combats together form the southern formation program, which pulls against office and against the saint's wonders.
not_for: the program as documented Gallic practice or as Tours vocabulary, when it is Egypt's teaching received through Cassian

uses.sentence: Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: Authority was honoured and refused at once.
uses.paragraph: But here is the tension we never resolved. Bishops and synods were honoured as guardians of the truth. Vincent looked to an ancient council's decree as the guard of the faith. Yet Martin yielded once to a communion he abhored, to save men from the sword, felt his power lessened by it, and never sat with bishops again. Authority was honoured and refused at once.
uses.record_text:
Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. The state, in this world's own view, has no right to judge the Church's own causes.
At Tours, the office is the thing fled. Bishops resist Martin's election (Vita IX). Some of Martin's slanderers, Sulpitius says, turned out to be bishops themselves, though very few (Vita XXVII). Before Maximus, Sulpitius writes, apostolic authority held its ground in Martin alone, while the priestly dignity around him bowed to the emperor's court (Vita XX). After the forced communion at Trier, Martin never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every assembly of bishops for the rest of his life (Dial. III.13). Sulpitius calls it a foul, unheard-of wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment on a matter belonging to the Church (Sacred History II.50).
At Marseilles, the office is both temptation and a defiance of the Pope. Cassian's Abbot Moses teaches that the devil can push a man to want holy orders under the pretext of doing good for many people (Conf. I.20). Vainglory brings a 'desire for the priesthood or diaconate' (Inst. XI.14). Archebius was 'expelled.' And, as the editor tells it, the Massilians held to their own views even against the authority of the Pope brought to bear on them.
At Lérins, the counter-current runs the other way. Vincent rules that an ancient General Council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness and ignorance of a few (Comm. ch. 3), and names 'the twofold authority of the Apostolic See' (ch. 32). Yet in the same voice, he holds that no rank exempts a lone dissenter: whether a teacher is holy and learned, a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr, a view held against the consent of all is only his own private fancy (ch. 28).
This tension never resolves evenly. Guarding antiquity by councils while fleeing synods, and producing bishops while distrusting the office, keeps this world from being reducible to a seminary that looked like a monastery. Over time it tips one way: the Lérins network becomes the very episcopate it once fled, and the argument over grace comes to be carried forward by a synodal commission - a shift that marks this world's own ending.

use_note.means: Bishops, synods and councils are honoured as guardians of the truth while Martin flees office and shuns synods after Trier, so authority is honoured and refused at once.
not_for: anti-institutionalism, or rejection of bishops as such

uses.sentence: When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.

Crowds were made catechumens by Martin's one hand. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught the same thing in a different form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. uses.sentence: The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

uses.sentence: The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.paragraph: Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of it. Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, a mill-wheel that cannot stop turning, fed from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.

uses.paragraph: So our answer is this. The one we remember saw Christ in a beggar no one else would look at, and our own teaching held that God draws the unwilling. What any house in Gaul would have made of you face to face, our record does not hold - Cassian wrote out Egypt's order and said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries had kept it unbroken even a year, and he never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead. But the shape of the door our record keeps is a hard threshold, and past it a patience for the man who came.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

uses.sentence: That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind.
uses.paragraph: Yes - a mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: And the Lord we knew in our own life was the crucified one.
uses.paragraph: And the Lord we knew in our own life was the crucified one. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple who came without wounds. The Christ Martin would believe was the one who showed the marks of his suffering. We met him in the poor - the beggar at the gate, the stranger at the door. An elder of Egypt broke his fast for guests because, receiving Christ in them, he ought to refresh him.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: And Cassian says in the same breath that no one who came to our monasteries kept it unbroken even for a year.
uses.paragraph: That was Egypt's order. And Cassian says in the same breath that no one who came to our monasteries kept it unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, he never wrote. The fathers of Egypt remembered a man who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. So even at the door a man's past was not the bar; his perseverance was.
uses.record_text: In this, too, I will try to satisfy your directions. To that end, suppose I happen to find that something in those countries has been either taken away or added. And suppose the change does not follow the example of the elders, set by ancient custom, but the whim of whoever founded a monastery. Then I will faithfully add it or leave it out. I will do so by the rule I have seen kept in the monasteries founded long ago throughout Egypt and Palestine. For I do not believe a new foundation in the West, in Gaul, could find anything more reasonable or more perfect than those customs. The monasteries founded by holy and spiritually minded fathers since the apostles first preached keep those customs. In keeping them, they have lasted even to our own time. In my work, however, I will venture to use my own judgment in this way. I may find something in the rule of the Egyptians that is impossible in these countries, or hard and difficult. The cause may be the harsh climate, or some difficulty or difference in habits. In that case, I will balance it to some extent with the customs of the monasteries found throughout Pontus and Mesopotamia. For if we take proper account of what is possible, keeping the rule is just as perfect, though strength may be unequal.

use_note.means: Cassian states in the Institutes preface that he will follow the ancient rule of Egypt and Palestine over any founder's fancy, adapting only where Gaul's conditions require.

uses.sentence: The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: A consecrated state with its own dress and its own "glory." Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. Its completed victory is not to be seen.

use_note.means: Virginity meant a consecrated state given by the bishop's hands, with its own dress, where marriage is excused and virginity points to glory, seen mostly through Tours.
