uses.sentence: The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.

uses.sentence: All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness

uses.sentence: An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.
uses.paragraph: The question you name as eternal fate was argued otherwise. Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it? Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour. Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.
uses.record_text: An outsider's word for a question we left beyond reason. Our own teacher never used it. But he called it blasphemy to think God wills only some, not all, to be saved.

use_note.means: Predestination was Augustine's word, not Cassian's, for what the Gallic brethren were in darkness on, though Cassian called it blasphemy to say God wills only some saved.

uses.sentence: What connects the customs to the apostles we said plainly: they aimed at what the apostles themselves reached, the perfection of love and the common life of the first Church.
uses.paragraph: What connects the customs to the apostles we said plainly: they aimed at what the apostles themselves reached, the perfection of love and the common life of the first Church. The apostolic is not first a chain of office but that charity. And at Tours the highest thing said of Martin was that he had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, before an emperor. Not a claim to their succession as bishops but to their virtue shown.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the highest thing said of Martin - having the apostles' power over death, demons, and emperors. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life.

uses.sentence: Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down".
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.record_text: For us tradition is what has been received from predecessors and must be passed on unchanged. Vincent's second criterion of truth after Scripture, "the Tradition of the Catholic Church." Pope Stephen's rule, "nothing but what has been handed down." Cassian's "traditions of the Elders" by which thoughts are judged. And the "steady tradition ... from antiquity" without which Martin will not honour a tomb.

use_note.means: Tradition meant what has been received and must be passed on unchanged, the ground on which Vincent's rule, Cassian's elders and Martin's refusal of a tomb are all judged.

uses.sentence: God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: Beyond the formula, this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us. Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in. God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy. The will stays free in us; and it is weak; and without his help given every day and hour it reaches nothing. Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society

uses.sentence: It was the act of turning, not an experience inside it.
uses.paragraph: No. For us conversion was not a single moment of inward change but the day a man turned to the monastic life. Among the brethren at Marseilles it named "the early days of their conversion" - bright at first, then cooling - and a murderer's "compulsory conversion" that became a voluntary one. uses.sentence: The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was not our sole authority. We held three things together: the canon of Scripture, the tradition of the Church, and the consent of the ancients. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly. The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers. What guards it is the tradition of the Catholic Church, and within that tradition the test is threefold: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. uses.sentence: After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.

And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

uses.sentence: Vincent looked to an ancient council's decree as the guard of the faith.
uses.paragraph: But here is the tension we never resolved. Bishops and synods were honoured as guardians of the truth. Vincent looked to an ancient council's decree as the guard of the faith. Yet Martin yielded once to a communion he abhored, to save men from the sword, felt his power lessened by it, and never sat with bishops again. Authority was honoured and refused at once.
uses.record_text:
Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. The state, in this world's own view, has no right to judge the Church's own causes.
At Tours, the office is the thing fled. Bishops resist Martin's election (Vita IX). Some of Martin's slanderers, Sulpitius says, turned out to be bishops themselves, though very few (Vita XXVII). Before Maximus, Sulpitius writes, apostolic authority held its ground in Martin alone, while the priestly dignity around him bowed to the emperor's court (Vita XX). After the forced communion at Trier, Martin never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every assembly of bishops for the rest of his life (Dial. III.13). Sulpitius calls it a foul, unheard-of wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment on a matter belonging to the Church (Sacred History II.50).
At Marseilles, the office is both temptation and a defiance of the Pope. Cassian's Abbot Moses teaches that the devil can push a man to want holy orders under the pretext of doing good for many people (Conf. I.20). Vainglory brings a 'desire for the priesthood or diaconate' (Inst. XI.14). Archebius was 'expelled.' And, as the editor tells it, the Massilians held to their own views even against the authority of the Pope brought to bear on them.
At Lérins, the counter-current runs the other way. Vincent rules that an ancient General Council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness and ignorance of a few (Comm. ch. 3), and names 'the twofold authority of the Apostolic See' (ch. 32). Yet in the same voice, he holds that no rank exempts a lone dissenter: whether a teacher is holy and learned, a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr, a view held against the consent of all is only his own private fancy (ch. 28).
This tension never resolves evenly. Guarding antiquity by councils while fleeing synods, and producing bishops while distrusting the office, keeps this world from being reducible to a seminary that looked like a monastery. Over time it tips one way: the Lérins network becomes the very episcopate it once fled, and the argument over grace comes to be carried forward by a synodal commission - a shift that marks this world's own ending.

use_note.means: Bishops, synods and councils are honoured as guardians of the truth while Martin flees office and shuns synods after Trier, so authority is honoured and refused at once.

uses.sentence: The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution, or therapy

uses.sentence: The grace of God always works together with our will; it goes before the will, helps it, and crowns it.
uses.paragraph: What the power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer showed us is this: it was Christ's power, not the saint's. Among the brethren at Marseilles the whole program was received from Egypt's elders as the fathers' own. The twelve psalms at evening and at night came, Cassian says, from the fathers of Egypt in the days when only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.

He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So yes - we held there was no other way to say it.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: We spoke of free will that always remains in a man, weak but real, able to neglect or delight in the grace of God.
uses.paragraph: We spoke of a debt that could not be paid, taken out of the way by Christ's cross. We spoke of free will that always remains in a man, weak but real, able to neglect or delight in the grace of God. And we spoke of God calling us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, drawing us toward salvation. Whether a child not yet able to choose carries guilt from birth - that question as you shape it is not in our record the way it stands in yours.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the power that "always remains free in man" to "neglect or delight in the grace of God." Real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour are truly his and truly required. Weak enough that "the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour." Never denied, never sufficient.

uses.sentence: Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
uses.paragraph: Beyond the formula, this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us. Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in. God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy. The will stays free in us; and it is weak; and without his help given every day and hour it reaches nothing. Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.

uses.sentence: At Tours Martin was ten when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen.
uses.paragraph: The question names a struggle - cannot manage to believe - and asks what we would say. Here is what our record lets us answer. We did not keep an argument for the unbeliever. No one among us wrote down a proof of the resurrection for someone who doubts it. What we kept instead was this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. At Tours Martin was ten when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is our one formation story, and it is one man's. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that grace kindles the first desire, not the will itself. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. And we held it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all to be saved. So what we would say is not that you must manage it, but that the calling comes first and the willing follows. We never told anyone they had to argue themselves into faith. We kept the catechumen a long time, watched what grace did, and counted the beginning of every good thought as God's. Beyond that our record does not reach - we have no treatise for the doubter, only the witness that grace draws the unwilling.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: Bishops and synods were honoured as guardians of the truth.
uses.paragraph: But here is the tension we never resolved. Bishops and synods were honoured as guardians of the truth. Vincent looked to an ancient council's decree as the guard of the faith. Yet Martin yielded once to a communion he abhored, to save men from the sword, felt his power lessened by it, and never sat with bishops again. Authority was honoured and refused at once.
uses.record_text:
Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. The state, in this world's own view, has no right to judge the Church's own causes.
At Tours, the office is the thing fled. Bishops resist Martin's election (Vita IX). Some of Martin's slanderers, Sulpitius says, turned out to be bishops themselves, though very few (Vita XXVII). Before Maximus, Sulpitius writes, apostolic authority held its ground in Martin alone, while the priestly dignity around him bowed to the emperor's court (Vita XX). After the forced communion at Trier, Martin never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every assembly of bishops for the rest of his life (Dial. III.13). Sulpitius calls it a foul, unheard-of wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment on a matter belonging to the Church (Sacred History II.50).
At Marseilles, the office is both temptation and a defiance of the Pope. Cassian's Abbot Moses teaches that the devil can push a man to want holy orders under the pretext of doing good for many people (Conf. I.20). Vainglory brings a 'desire for the priesthood or diaconate' (Inst. XI.14). Archebius was 'expelled.' And, as the editor tells it, the Massilians held to their own views even against the authority of the Pope brought to bear on them.
At Lérins, the counter-current runs the other way. Vincent rules that an ancient General Council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness and ignorance of a few (Comm. ch. 3), and names 'the twofold authority of the Apostolic See' (ch. 32). Yet in the same voice, he holds that no rank exempts a lone dissenter: whether a teacher is holy and learned, a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr, a view held against the consent of all is only his own private fancy (ch. 28).
This tension never resolves evenly. Guarding antiquity by councils while fleeing synods, and producing bishops while distrusting the office, keeps this world from being reducible to a seminary that looked like a monastery. Over time it tips one way: the Lérins network becomes the very episcopate it once fled, and the argument over grace comes to be carried forward by a synodal commission - a shift that marks this world's own ending.

uses.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, after the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The psalms themselves were learned by heart and said at the work, so that the mill of the mind, which cannot stop turning, is fed with what it ought to grind. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, a number the fathers of Egypt received from an angel who sang the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished. The book was the grain the wheel was meant to turn on. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. That too was done with the psalms in the mouth.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles it named "the early days of their conversion" - bright at first, then cooling - and a murderer's "compulsory conversion" that became a voluntary one.
uses.paragraph: No. For us conversion was not a single moment of inward change but the day a man turned to the monastic life. Among the brethren at Marseilles it named "the early days of their conversion" - bright at first, then cooling - and a murderer's "compulsory conversion" that became a voluntary one. It was the act of turning, not an experience inside it. At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

It is the act of turning to the monastic life: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one." At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

Nothing in the ground I am given to answer from this turn - and nothing else in the whole of our record as I hold it - speaks of any account of our worship obtained under torture. The brethren at Tours, as Sulpitius tells their life, kept the hours of prayer without a gap, and Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for those hours - the Spirit at the third, the Sacrifice at the sixth, the descent into hell at the ninth. Of the island's own day - a rule kept, an office sung - nothing. And the three whole books and conferences on the body's discipline were cut from the one edition I can read by a nineteenth-century hand, not by our own silence.

uses.sentence: And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant the whole body of Egyptian practice Cassian carried to a Gallic bishop's new house, received from the fathers, not his own Rule.
not_for: a codified Rule such as Benedict's, or the Institutes as a theology textbook
Vincent's rule of faith, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule

uses.sentence: At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance.
uses.paragraph: The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.

uses.sentence: The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: But the clothes he took off are handed over to the care of the steward. They are kept until the excellence of his progress, his life and his endurance can be recognized through different kinds of temptations and trials.

use_note.means: Cassian explains in Institutes IV.6 that a novice's worldly clothes are kept by the steward until trials have proven his progress.
not_for: a claim that the clothes are kept permanently, when the chapter says they are given away once progress is proven

uses.sentence: A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house.
uses.paragraph: The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

uses.sentence: The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road.
uses.paragraph: The forced communion at Treves. The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us. Here is what happened. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives

uses.sentence: Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried. The books were read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were not inventions of ours. They were already the faith believed everywhere, always, by all when our own span opened. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was what those books gave us: the cloak story as Sulpitius told it, with the Lord's own words set beside it - what is done to the least of these is done to him. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something. The hours of prayer themselves, built around the hours of the Lord's passion - the third hour when the Spirit came down, the sixth when the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, the ninth when he went down into hell.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
Cassian's received customs and whether Gallic houses kept them, which sit in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries, or Benedict's Rule

uses.sentence: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains.
uses.paragraph: And when the sword was drawn? Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains. He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When anger failed, the emperor named executioners. Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: To stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, Martin yields once to a communion he abhors, is told by an angel that his compunction is just, feels his power diminished, and never attends a synod again.

use_note.means: Gallus tells that Martin yielded once to communion with the Ithacian bishops to save men from the tribunes, then lost power, was told his compunction was just, and shunned synods.
not_for: a motive of grief for Martin's silence about it, when Gallus gives the character of the times, as in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains

uses.sentence: That was the first lesson, before any other.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution, or therapy
public penance for a committed fault, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
the virtue that regulates all others on the royal road, which sits in gallic.term.discretion
a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. The trouble was not soldiers hunting believers. It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.record_text: The bishops had given way weakly. They let the royal court outrank the priesthood's own dignity. But Martin alone still held the authority handed down from the apostles.

use_note.means: Sulpitius writes in the Life of Martin that while bishops fawned on the emperor Maximus, apostolic authority still asserted itself in Martin alone.
not_for: Martin's own claim about himself, when it is Sulpitius's verdict
a fair report of every bishop at Maximus's court

uses.sentence: The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's

uses.sentence: The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour.
uses.paragraph: The question you name as eternal fate was argued otherwise. Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it? Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour. Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the power that "always remains free in man" to "neglect or delight in the grace of God." Real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour are truly his and truly required. Weak enough that "the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour." Never denied, never sufficient.

use_note.means: Free will meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, a real but weak power that always remains in man, which grace strengthens without removing and which never suffices alone.
not_for: a philosophical question about determinism
the Pelagian half of a grace-versus-works binary
grace as such, which sits in gallic.term.grace
a Tours teaching, whose literature does not raise the matter

uses.sentence: No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to the Lord was the books, read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.

uses.sentence: The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - the whole southern formation program: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing without the vocabulary - Martin's discernment of Anatolius's robe and of the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV) - but 'no "purity of heart," no "discretion," no fault-list.' Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. Two of Cassian's own conferences on this program, on chastity and on nocturnal illusions, and one book of the Institutes, do not survive in the English edition this account draws on.

use_note.means: Purity of heart as goal, discretion as regulator and the eight faults as combats together form the southern formation program, which pulls against office and against the saint's wonders.

uses.sentence: All of it served one mark.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

uses.sentence: The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see.
uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.
uses.record_text: Martin was called to become bishop of the church at Tours. But he could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. So a man named Ruricius, one of the townspeople, pretended that his wife was ill. He threw himself down at Martin's knees and persuaded him to come out. Crowds of townspeople had already been posted along the road Martin traveled. So he was taken to the city under a kind of guard. An unbelievable number of people had gathered, in a marvelous way, to cast their votes. They came not only from that town, but from the nearby cities too. Everyone had one wish and the same prayers. All held the same firm view: Martin was most worthy to be bishop, and the church would be happy with such a bishop. A few people, however, were resisting in an ungodly way. Among them were some of the bishops who had been called in to appoint the new bishop. They claimed, if you please, that Martin was a contemptible person, unworthy to be bishop. He had a despicable face, they said, shabby clothes, and disgusting hair. People of sounder judgment laughed at this madness of theirs. For while these objectors tried to slander the man, they only proclaimed how outstanding he was.

use_note.means: Sulpitius narrates how Martin was drawn to Tours by a ruse, acclaimed bishop by crowds, and opposed by some bishops who scorned his appearance.
not_for: a neutral account of the objectors, when Sulpitius openly opposed them
