uses.sentence: So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed.
uses.paragraph: Yes - a mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested

uses.sentence: About the sixth hour the real trial comes.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the sixth fault, "which we may term weariness or distress of heart," "especially trying to solitaries." The noon assault that "produces dislike of the place, disgust with the cell, and disdain and contempt of the brethren." It makes the monk gaze at the sun "as if it was too slow in setting," and dresses his escape as pious duty until "the soldier of Christ becomes a runaway from His service, and a deserter."

use_note.means: Accidie meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, the noonday weariness that assails a monk in his cell as the sixth fault and ends in desertion unless he stays.
not_for: sloth as laziness, or depression and burnout as clinical conditions

uses.sentence: He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall.
uses.paragraph: The forced communion at Treves. The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us. Here is what happened. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

uses.sentence: At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed.
uses.paragraph: At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.

The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant the man himself, cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.
not_for: a cloistered religious under a written Rule, or Benedictine and later medieval monasticism
someone who by definition is not a soldier, a bishop or a city dweller

uses.sentence: And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
Cassian's received customs and whether Gallic houses kept them, which sit in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries, or Benedict's Rule
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: For us the typical failure of a monk is not apostasy but cooling. The novice who "grow[s] cold in regard to the rule." The renunciant "turned out a deserter or lukewarm." The elders who "pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth." The Sarabaites "cast down into hell by the lukewarmness of their purpose." A disease of temperature that damns.

use_note.means: Lukewarmness meant the monk's characteristic failure, cooling rather than apostasy, a disease of temperature that damns and that a grey head does not cure.
not_for: mild disapproval, half-heartedness, or burnout as an understandable phase

a word for monks only, when Salvian uses it of ordinary Christians

uses.sentence: The fathers' remedy: stay.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the sixth fault, "which we may term weariness or distress of heart," "especially trying to solitaries." The noon assault that "produces dislike of the place, disgust with the cell, and disdain and contempt of the brethren." It makes the monk gaze at the sun "as if it was too slow in setting," and dresses his escape as pious duty until "the soldier of Christ becomes a runaway from His service, and a deserter."

use_note.means: Accidie meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, the noonday weariness that assails a monk in his cell as the sixth fault and ends in desertion unless he stays.
not_for: sloth as laziness, or depression and burnout as clinical conditions
a Gallic coinage, when Cassian gives the name and the midday demon as the teaching of Egypt's elders
the general cooling of fervour, which sits in gallic.term.lukewarmness
the list of faults as a whole, which sits in gallic.term.eight-principal-faults

uses.sentence: We did not read them the way you are reading them now.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested
the mill-wheel of thoughts fed by psalms learned by heart, which sits in gallic.term.thoughts

uses.sentence: Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought.
uses.paragraph: What belongs with that is the shape of what happened next. The churches came for the men who had left them. A bishop's see was capture, not achievement. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought. The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see. So what a man gave up to join us did not mean he was done with the world's claims on him.
uses.record_text: A monk is lured out of his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife is ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes and disgusting hair, and answered by a psalm opened at random.

use_note.means: Sulpitius reports that Martin was lured from his monastery by a pretext, escorted under guard, and made bishop of Tours though some bishops objected to his mean clothes.
not_for: a neutral account of the objecting bishops, when Sulpitius is hostile to them

uses.sentence: He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty, stated by Cassian for custom, Vincent for doctrine and Martin for cult, though none cites another.
not_for: growth of doctrine without alteration, which sits in gallic.term.progress-vs-alteration
the test as consistently applied, when that is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity

uses.sentence: The elder cut the office short and answered with a field.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: Two friends come back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - and the elder shortens the office to answer them with a husbandman, the rain, and "the initiative ... comes from God."

use_note.means: Cassian records that Germanus, troubled at morning prayer by one sentence of Chaeremon's, drew from the elder the husbandman answer that the initiative to do good comes from God.
not_for: Cassian's doctrine of grace at depth, which sits in gallic.term.grace
a Tours doctrine of grace, which the record does not hold

uses.sentence: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives
the communion Martin yielded to and the angel, which sit in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-forced-communion-and-the-angel
an event corroborated outside Sulpitius's own writings

uses.sentence: Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

use_note.means: Sulpitius records Martin, at a donative before battle, telling Julian Caesar he is now Christ's soldier and offering to stand unarmed, whereupon the enemy surrenders without bloodshed.
not_for: the cloak scene and Martin's years as an unbaptized catechumen, which sit in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.term.catechumen
Cassian's dress-mysticism soldier, which sits in gallic.term.soldier-of-christ
the editors' identification of Julian and Worms as the text's own

uses.sentence: The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried. The books were read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were not inventions of ours. They were already the faith believed everywhere, always, by all when our own span opened. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was what those books gave us: the cloak story as Sulpitius told it, with the Lord's own words set beside it - what is done to the least of these is done to him. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something. The hours of prayer themselves, built around the hours of the Lord's passion - the third hour when the Spirit came down, the sixth when the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, the ninth when he went down into hell.
uses.record_text: The one question our whole argument about grace turns on. Does God have mercy on us because we first showed a good will? Or does our good will begin because God first had mercy?

use_note.means: The beginning of a good will named the point at issue in the grace argument, whether the will starts with us or with God, which Cassian answered on both sides.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position that man makes the first move
either of Cassian's two phrasings taken as his one position, a contest carried in gallic.contested.beginning-of-good-will
the broader doctrine of grace, which sits in gallic.term.grace
the beginning of the monastic life, which sits in gallic.term.conversion

uses.sentence: Sulpitius told it, and it is our one whole story.
uses.paragraph: How did Martin come to believe? Sulpitius told it, and it is our one whole story. At ten, against his parents' wish, Martin went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Why he went at ten, what moved him, Sulpitius never said. The one thing given is that he went before he believed it, and stayed there years.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.
not_for: Vincent on Scripture's canon, its sufficiency and its need of the Church's reading, which sit in gallic.limit.no-one-who-saw-him
Chaeremon's two-sided answer on grace and Vincent's reading of the Apostolic See's letter, which sit in gallic.contested.beginning-of-good-will and gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity

the sixth-hour death, the bystanders' laughter and Martin at Trier, which sit in gallic.dw.the-christ-who-bears-the-wounds, gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion
a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, or any claim about what guests later said, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.paragraph: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus reports that Martin refused to remove Brictio from the presbyterate when he was accused of crimes, lest he seem to avenge himself, saying Christ bore with Judas.
not_for: a verdict that the charges against Brictio were false, which the passage never gives
a claim about Brictio's later career or status, which nothing at this locus supports

uses.sentence: Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
sincerity or good intentions
the end, the kingdom, which sits in gallic.term.goal-and-end

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule.
uses.paragraph: We read to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The purpose was not learning but living. The fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. uses.sentence: We held him as God - Vincent's formula from the island: in God one substance but three Persons, in Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh.
uses.paragraph: Jesus was the crucified one who met us in the poor, and the Lord whose grace drew us while we were still unwilling. We held him as God - Vincent's formula from the island: in God one substance but three Persons, in Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh. At the hours we kept what Cassian handed us from Egypt: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

uses.sentence: He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized.
uses.paragraph: We kept one story of how a man came to believe, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

We never make that claim - we say Cassian hands the fathers' story down, and Piamun told it - but a participant who heard us as asserting the events would find no historian willing to say they did. The stories are kept as formation literature, not as checked history. That Martin's diminished power after the Ithacian communion is a fact anyone can weigh. uses.sentence: The founder went unafraid onto an island shunned for its squalor and its serpents, carrying a psalm; the serpents gave way; a camp of God rose where no one would live.
uses.paragraph: Of the island's own day — a rule kept, a novice received, an elder's saying, an office sung — nothing. The founder went unafraid onto an island shunned for its squalor and its serpents, carrying a psalm; the serpents gave way; a camp of God rose where no one would live. That is a disciple's funeral sermon, read only as far as its words can be read. What the rooms looked like, what we ate, where we slept — only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.sentence: The remedy is to stay.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the sixth fault, "which we may term weariness or distress of heart," "especially trying to solitaries." The noon assault that "produces dislike of the place, disgust with the cell, and disdain and contempt of the brethren." It makes the monk gaze at the sun "as if it was too slow in setting," and dresses his escape as pious duty until "the soldier of Christ becomes a runaway from His service, and a deserter."

use_note.means: Accidie meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, the noonday weariness that assails a monk in his cell as the sixth fault and ends in desertion unless he stays.

uses.sentence: After he raised a dead catechumen, the man told of a tribunal where two angels sent him back.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the saint's power was shown for the countryside people, the Gallic rustics who had scarcely heard the name of Christ. He halted idols, burned temples, and built churches where they fell. A whole crowd was made catechumens by his one hand. And Martin himself stayed a catechumen for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak. After he raised a dead catechumen, the man told of a tribunal where two angels sent him back. Tours kept no teaching on who was saved; it kept the saint's labor for the unconverted, and one man's glimpse past death.
uses.record_text: Martin returns to find a catechumen dead and unbaptized. He bolts the door and stretches himself on the body. He perceives that power is present, and two hours later the man opens his eyes. Afterward the man tells of the tribunal and the two angels that sent him back.

use_note.means: Sulpitius reports that Martin found a catechumen dead unbaptized, stretched himself on the body, perceived power present, and saw the man revive to tell of the tribunal and the angels.

uses.sentence: He wills none of his little ones to perish, and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the one thing we set against grievous blasphemy was this: to think that God does not will all men to be saved. He wills none of his little ones to perish, and those who perish, perish against his will. That was Abbot Chaeremon's word, as Cassian carried it from Egypt, on the God who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation. So we refused the thought that he chose some and passed the rest by. We called it blasphemy to say it.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

uses.sentence: Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us.
uses.paragraph: The question you name as eternal fate was argued otherwise. Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it? Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour. Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.

No account survives from any brother expelled in error, or from any who felt their superior bore with them when they should have been heard. uses.sentence: The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ.
uses.paragraph: The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant the man himself, cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.
not_for: a cloistered religious under a written Rule, or Benedictine and later medieval monasticism

uses.sentence: An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.
uses.paragraph: What we had instead of a chain from the apostles was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. A dead man breathed at the saint's prayer. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. The connection was the books, and the power that made the books real.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: A thought one is ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.
uses.paragraph: Inside the house, authority was the elder's judgment standing in for the junior's own. Every thought was laid bare to the senior the moment it rose, before any deed. A thought one is ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. At Tours there was one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics. At Marseilles Cassian named "Abbot" as the title of every Egyptian father he reported.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.

uses.sentence: A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty, stated by Cassian for custom, Vincent for doctrine and Martin for cult, though none cites another.
not_for: growth of doctrine without alteration, which sits in gallic.term.progress-vs-alteration

uses.sentence: The countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak.
uses.paragraph: Where the account of someone we failed, or turned away, or harmed would be - a novice scorned too long, a woman's word unheard, a crowd met with curses - our record is silent. The countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak. The women of both houses left no word. The bishops who objected to Martin at the election are heard only through the man who called them ridiculous. So the honest answer is this. A failure named and answered, in the voice of the one we failed, is not in our record to give.
uses.record_text: Foreknowing his death, Martin goes to make peace among quarrelling clerics. He sickens, and refuses straw for his bed of sackcloth and ashes rather than set his disciples a softer example. He is carried to burial by two thousand monks, old men and young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins.

use_note.means: Sulpitius tells Bassula that Martin, foreknowing his death, went to make peace at Condate, died refusing straw, and was buried by two thousand monks and a choir of virgins.
not_for: an eyewitness account, when Sulpitius disclaims being present

uses.sentence: No.
uses.paragraph: No. For us conversion was not a single moment of inward change but the day a man turned to the monastic life. Among the brethren at Marseilles it named "the early days of their conversion" - bright at first, then cooling - and a murderer's "compulsory conversion" that became a voluntary one. It was the act of turning, not an experience inside it. At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, "conversion" is not a change of religion. It is the act of turning to the monastic life: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one." At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

use_note.means: Conversion meant, at Marseilles, the act of turning to the monastic life and not a change of religion, while at Tours it meant turning to Christ.

uses.sentence: Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is one man's own confession, made alone.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.
not_for: a Gallic treatise on the atonement, which no one in this world wrote

uses.sentence: The book was the grain the wheel was meant to turn on.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, after the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The psalms themselves were learned by heart and said at the work, so that the mill of the mind, which cannot stop turning, is fed with what it ought to grind. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, a number the fathers of Egypt received from an angel who sang the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished. The book was the grain the wheel was meant to turn on. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. That too was done with the psalms in the mouth.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested
the mill-wheel of thoughts fed by psalms learned by heart, which sits in gallic.term.thoughts

uses.sentence: Salvian of Marseilles wrote of a city he knew, sacked again and again by barbarian raiders, its dead left unburied in the streets - and then reported that the surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games.
uses.paragraph: And there is this. Salvian of Marseilles wrote of a city he knew, sacked again and again by barbarian raiders, its dead left unburied in the streets - and then reported that the surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games. He wrote against the rich who were murdering the poor with taxes, grinding them until they fled to the barbarians or rose in revolt. That uprising our own officials called rebellion. We who had renounced the world to serve God in the desert or the cell - we said almost nothing of it. Salvian is the one voice among us who named what the countryside poor were suffering. The rest of us kept silence, or spoke of them only as a mission field. That, too, unsettles - not because what Salvian said was contested, but because he was nearly alone in saying it.
uses.record_text: A presbyter of Marseilles, writing of a city he knew, describes what he himself saw after its repeated sack by barbarian raiders - the dead left unburied in the streets - and then reports that the city's own surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games.

use_note.means: Salvian reports seeing the unburied dead of a repeatedly sacked city and then its surviving notables petitioning the emperors for circus games, evidencing his charge that judgment is present.

uses.sentence: So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: For us "the world" is what a monk has left - kin, property, honours, delights, "secular business." We name it from the far side of the renunciation, as a warfare one has been discharged from and a sea one has come out of. We never name it as a place from which God is absent.

use_note.means: The world meant what a monk has left, kin, property, honours and business, named from the harbour as a warfare one was discharged from, never as a place without God.
not_for: secular in the modern sense of non-religious or secular government
contempt for the created order, or misanthropy
