uses.sentence: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - the whole southern formation program: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing without the vocabulary - Martin's discernment of Anatolius's robe and of the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV) - but 'no "purity of heart," no "discretion," no fault-list.' Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. Two of Cassian's own conferences on this program, on chastity and on nocturnal illusions, and one book of the Institutes, do not survive in the English edition this account draws on.

use_note.means: Purity of heart as goal, discretion as regulator and the eight faults as combats together form the southern formation program, which pulls against office and against the saint's wonders.
not_for: the program as documented Gallic practice or as Tours vocabulary, when it is Egypt's teaching received through Cassian

uses.sentence: Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies.
uses.paragraph: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.
uses.record_text: These things filled the wretched man with bitter rage. And, I believe, the urging of those demons drove him most of all. He attacked Martin so fiercely that he barely held back from striking him. The holy man, for his part, kept a calm face and a peaceful mind. With gentle words he tried to hold back the unhappy man's madness. But the spirit of evil had such a grip on him that he could not control even his own mind. That mind was a very foolish one even at the best of times. His lips trembled, and his face changed, pale with rage. He poured out sinful words. He claimed he was a holier man than Martin, who had raised him. From his earliest years, he said, he had grown up in the monastery, trained in the Church's holy ways. Martin, he said, had first been stained by a soldier's life, as Martin could not deny. And now, he said, Martin had sunk completely into old age's foolishness. His groundless superstitions and ridiculous fancies about visions had brought him to it.

use_note.means: Gallus describes Brictio nearly assaulting Martin and claiming to be holier for growing up in the monastery, while Martin answered with gentle words.
not_for: a neutral report of Brictio's case, when it comes from men hostile to him
the reproof that provoked the outburst, which sits in gallic.quote.brictio-horses-and-slaves
a claim that Martin argued back, when the text gives him only gentle restraint
the courtyard scene and Brictio's repentance, which sit in gallic.story.brictio-in-the-courtyard

uses.sentence: He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him.
uses.paragraph: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus reports that Martin refused to remove Brictio from the presbyterate when he was accused of crimes, lest he seem to avenge himself, saying Christ bore with Judas.
not_for: a verdict that the charges against Brictio were false, which the passage never gives
a claim about Brictio's later career or status, which nothing at this locus supports
the courtyard tirade and Martin's restraint, which sit in gallic.quote.brictio-tirade-and-martins-restraint
Martin's saying as a verbatim transcript rather than words a narrator reports him repeating

uses.sentence: The man who cut his cloak for the unpitied became a monk, then fled the office of bishop and was seized into it, and died refusing straw for his deathbed so as not to set his disciples a softer example.
uses.paragraph: That soldier was Martin, still a catechumen, years before he left Caesar's service at a donative and said, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. The man who cut his cloak for the unpitied became a monk, then fled the office of bishop and was seized into it, and died refusing straw for his deathbed so as not to set his disciples a softer example. He was buried by two thousand monks and a choir of virgins.
uses.record_text: Foreknowing his death, Martin goes to make peace among quarrelling clerics. He sickens, and refuses straw for his bed of sackcloth and ashes rather than set his disciples a softer example. He is carried to burial by two thousand monks, old men and young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins.

use_note.means: Sulpitius tells Bassula that Martin, foreknowing his death, went to make peace at Condate, died refusing straw, and was buried by two thousand monks and a choir of virgins.
not_for: an eyewitness account, when Sulpitius disclaims being present
the later cult of Martin at Tours, which lies outside the window
the south's teaching on death or judgment, which sits in gallic.term.fear-hope-love
the funeral-as-triumph passage verbatim, which sits in gallic.quote.martin-funeral-triumph-contrast

uses.sentence: He says only that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance a year.
uses.paragraph: That is Egypt's door. What a house in Gaul did with a man who came to its own threshold, Cassian never wrote. He says only that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance a year. Whether any house in Gaul scorned a newcomer at the door for ten days, or searched him for a coin, or lodged him a year under the guest-elder, our record does not hold.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant the whole body of Egyptian practice Cassian carried to a Gallic bishop's new house, received from the fathers, not his own Rule.
not_for: a codified Rule such as Benedict's, or the Institutes as a theology textbook
Vincent's rule of faith, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule
the content of one custom, such as the psalm system in gallic.term.unceasing-prayer or the dress in gallic.term.the-monks-dress
documented Gallic practice, when Cassian admits no one in our monasteries kept Egypt's perseverance unbroken even for a year

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the virtue the fathers of Egypt put before all others - before reading, before silence, before even humility - was obedience.
uses.paragraph: There was space for obedience before certainty. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the virtue the fathers of Egypt put before all others - before reading, before silence, before even humility - was obedience. A junior learned it first by orders contrary to his liking, the conquest of his own wishes. That teaching never required a man to say he was certain. It required him to do what the elder said, to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose, and to let the elder's judgment stand in for his own. The fathers knew a man's own judgment could not be trusted alone - they called discretion the royal road between excess and slackness, where extremes meet. So a brother struggling with doubt would have been taught to bring the doubt to the elder, not to resolve it by himself.
uses.record_text: For us obedience is the virtue the Egyptians "put not merely before manual labour and reading and silence and quietness in the cell, but even before all virtues." It is proved by absurd and terrible commands - a dry stick watered for a year, a son carried to the river - and it is the first thing a junior learns, "to conquer his own wishes." At Tours it is what Sulpitius feels before Martin: "unlawful to do anything but acquiesce."

use_note.means: Obedience meant the virtue Egypt's fathers put before all others, proved by hard commands and learned first by the junior as conquering his own wishes.
not_for: blind obedience as the suppression of conscience
the dry stick and the river as abuse or cult control
whom one obeys as an office, which sits in gallic.term.elder-senior-abbot
a documented Gallic testing of juniors by contrary orders, which the record does not hold

uses.sentence: The apostolic is not first a chain of office but that charity.
uses.paragraph: What connects the customs to the apostles we said plainly: they aimed at what the apostles themselves reached, the perfection of love and the common life of the first Church. The apostolic is not first a chain of office but that charity. And at Tours the highest thing said of Martin was that he had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, before an emperor. Not a claim to their succession as bishops but to their virtue shown.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the highest thing said of Martin - having the apostles' power over death, demons, and emperors. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life.

use_note.means: Apostolic authority meant, at Tours, Martin's apostle-like power shown in raising the dead and facing an emperor, and at Marseilles the perfection of love and the first Church's common life.
not_for: apostolic succession of validly ordained bishops, or Martin's apostolic authority as jurisdiction
Rome as such, which sits in gallic.term.apostolic-see-pope
the saint's power as such, which sits in gallic.term.virtus

uses.sentence: A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution, or therapy
public penance for a committed fault, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
the virtue that regulates all others on the royal road, which sits in gallic.term.discretion
a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: A consecrated state with its own dress and its own "glory." Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. Its completed victory is not to be seen.

use_note.means: Virginity meant a consecrated state given by the bishop's hands, with its own dress, where marriage is excused and virginity points to glory, seen mostly through Tours.
not_for: virginity as sexual abstinence merely, or as repression
nuns under a later rule
the south's own teaching on chastity, which was cut from the vendored English edition
purity of heart as the monk's goal, which sits in gallic.term.purity-of-heart

uses.sentence: Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

use_note.means: Novelty and antiquity named the axis on which all three founding voices judged legitimacy: the new is suspect for being new, and what was handed down is held fast.
not_for: novelty as harmless newness or as a virtue
conservative as a political posture
the three-part procedure, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule
Vincent's growth analogy, which sits in gallic.term.progress-vs-alteration

uses.sentence: Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
sincerity or good intentions
the end, the kingdom, which sits in gallic.term.goal-and-end
the south's own chastity teaching, since Conference XII is excised from the vendored edition

uses.sentence: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply.
uses.paragraph: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.
uses.record_text: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood storms into the courtyard. He calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then repents within the hour. Martin will not remove him, saying he bears with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas.

use_note.means: Gallus relates that Brictio, raised by Martin, stormed at him and called his visions ridiculous fancies, repented within the hour, and was borne with as Christ bore Judas.
not_for: a neutral report of Brictio's case, when it comes from men hostile to him

uses.sentence: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt.
uses.paragraph: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt. The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received. At Tours the hours themselves are not described, but Martin's practice is: prayer without a gap, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested
the mill-wheel of thoughts fed by psalms learned by heart, which sits in gallic.term.thoughts
reading of Scripture or lessons at the hours, which this record does not hold

uses.sentence: Not the two houses at Marseilles.
uses.paragraph: Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Our record holds no excavation, no building plan, no stones counted. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature
the island's founder, his arrival and his going to a see, which sit in gallic.story.honoratus-and-the-island
what the brethren at Tours sang and at what hours, which sits in gallic.term.unceasing-prayer
the unheard women of the houses, whose one trace, a choir of virgins, sits in gallic.story.death-of-martin-at-condate

uses.sentence: The faith believed everywhere, always, by all is kept by holding to the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher - be he bishop, be he confessor, be he martyr.
uses.paragraph: We never agreed that anyone settled it. Our whole grammar ran the other way. The faith believed everywhere, always, by all is kept by holding to the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher - be he bishop, be he confessor, be he martyr. Vincent, on the island, wrote that test down against his own forgetting: when a part dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty appears, hold fast to antiquity; when a few stand against many, prefer the decree of an ancient council or, failing that, the collated writings of the fathers. Not one man's judgment, not one see's, but the consent of those who came before us. What is new - a doctrine, a custom, a cult - is suspect for being new. What was handed down from antiquity is held fast.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
Cassian's received customs and whether Gallic houses kept them, which sit in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries, or Benedict's Rule
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: Salvian wrote of unburied dead and a petition for games.
uses.paragraph: The texts themselves. Vincent wrote what he wrote about everywhere, always, by all. Cassian carried Egypt's customs west and said no Gallic house kept them a year. Sulpitius told of Martin at a city gate, at an election, and at Trier. The angel fixed twelve psalms, as Cassian hands the fathers' story down. Salvian wrote of unburied dead and a petition for games. A scholar could check each sentence we speak against the page it cites, and the words would be there.
uses.record_text: A presbyter of Marseilles, writing of a city he knew, describes what he himself saw after its repeated sack by barbarian raiders - the dead left unburied in the streets - and then reports that the city's own surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games.

use_note.means: Salvian reports seeing the unburied dead of a repeatedly sacked city and then its surviving notables petitioning the emperors for circus games, evidencing his charge that judgment is present.
not_for: the general pattern of lay worship against the games, which sits in gallic.term.church-or-circus

uses.sentence: Within the Catholic Church we must hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: And we held this: the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, yet it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. On the island Vincent made that the center of his rule. Within the Catholic Church we must hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Scripture is tested by tradition - not replaced by it, but read inside the consent of the fathers. Where a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, we prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

uses.sentence: More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to the Lord was the books, read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
the cloak vision or the raised catechumen as evidence that the Lord rose, when they show the saint's power, as in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.raising-of-the-catechumen
the content of Cassian's seven books against Nestorius, which is unread
a chain of witnesses, when the world's floor stands more than three centuries after the events

uses.sentence: What Martin kept hidden was not himself but one story - the affair at Treves and the communion he yielded to, which he hid because of the times.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin himself said that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding blood - in hunger, watchings, nakedness, and fasting. What Martin kept hidden was not himself but one story - the affair at Treves and the communion he yielded to, which he hid because of the times. He kept it from everyone but us, not because hiding was necessary for survival but because he never forgave himself the price. The secrecy was his own grief, not a general danger. Our record holds no catacombs, no underground gatherings, no flight from soldiers. What it holds instead is a monk who left Caesar's service and gathered brethren openly across the river from a city, and houses at Marseilles that sent their trained men to fill the churches' sees. If you are asking about another people's hiding in another age, that is not our own.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. uses.sentence: At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

uses.sentence: Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk.
uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.

uses.sentence: The fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it.
uses.paragraph: We read to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The purpose was not learning but living. The fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So the psalms keep the mill fed with what is good. The immediate goal of the whole life is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every practice is ranked by whether it serves that mark.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, a mill-wheel that cannot stop turning, fed from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.

uses.record_text: To stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, Martin yields once to a communion he abhors, is told by an angel that his compunction is just, feels his power diminished, and never attends a synod again.

uses.sentence: Martin went to the court to stop it.
uses.paragraph: The forced communion at Treves. The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us. Here is what happened. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.

uses.sentence: He halted idols, burned temples, and built churches where they fell.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the saint's power was shown for the countryside people, the Gallic rustics who had scarcely heard the name of Christ. He halted idols, burned temples, and built churches where they fell. A whole crowd was made catechumens by his one hand. And Martin himself stayed a catechumen for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak. After he raised a dead catechumen, the man told of a tribunal where two angels sent him back. Tours kept no teaching on who was saved; it kept the saint's labor for the unconverted, and one man's glimpse past death.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the unconverted countryside of Gaul. It was Martin's mission field. There he halted the veiled idols, burned temples, felled a sacred pine, and built churches where they fell.

use_note.means: Heathen rustics meant, at Tours, the unconverted Gallic countryside where Martin halted idols, burned temples and built churches where they fell.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught, and Cassian set it down, that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: What we held about how a man comes to faith is this: the beginning of it is not ours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught, and Cassian set it down, that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative, before a good will even rises, comes from God. That is not the whole of it, but it is the first thing: the drawing comes before the turning.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.
not_for: a settled verdict that the teaching is semi-Pelagian, when that label is contested
the claim that grace looks for human effort, which sits in gallic.quote.chaeremon-grace-requires-our-effort
a complete theory of how grace and free will fit together, when Chaeremon calls that beyond human grasp

uses.sentence: And we held this: the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, yet it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
uses.paragraph: And we held this: the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, yet it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. On the island Vincent made that the center of his rule. Within the Catholic Church we must hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Scripture is tested by tradition - not replaced by it, but read inside the consent of the fathers. Where a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, we prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.

uses.sentence: We confessed at the hours that the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid.
uses.paragraph: We confessed at the hours that the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid. That debt belonged to us. We said it could not be paid without him. But whether that debt is carried from birth, or comes only with a person's own willing and acting, our record does not say. The one thing Cassian states plainly is that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread
the saying that denying God wills all to be saved is grievous blasphemy, which sits in gallic.quote.grievous-blasphemy-not-all-men-to-be-saved

uses.sentence: A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death.
uses.paragraph: The forced communion at Treves. The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us. Here is what happened. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus

a separate witness from gallic.quote.aloof-from-assemblies-of-bishops, whose sentence closes this passage

uses.sentence: Of what you would find by digging there, our books say nothing — they dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the place was a wooden cell where Martin prayed, caves around it for the brethren, and a rude little stool such as those in use by the lowest of servants. Of what you would find by digging there, our books say nothing — they dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature

uses.sentence: Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one.
uses.paragraph: And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. Our record does not speak of being born again. It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society
the day of entry, which sits in gallic.term.conversion

uses.sentence: By "consent" Vincent meant an ancient council where one had spoken, or else the collated writings of the fathers - not one teacher alone, however great, but many together.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was not our sole authority. We held three things together: the canon of Scripture, the tradition of the Church, and the consent of the ancients. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly. The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers. What guards it is the tradition of the Catholic Church, and within that tradition the test is threefold: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. By "consent" Vincent meant an ancient council where one had spoken, or else the collated writings of the fathers - not one teacher alone, however great, but many together.

uses.sentence: And on the island, of a day kept there - the rising, the office, the work, the meals - our record holds nothing at all.
uses.paragraph: And on the island, of a day kept there - the rising, the office, the work, the meals - our record holds nothing at all.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.

uses.sentence: The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
sincerity or good intentions

uses.sentence: After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
