uses.sentence: The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us.
uses.paragraph: The forced communion at Treves. The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us. Here is what happened. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.

uses.sentence: The fathers, not one man - living old men for Cassian, collated doctors for Vincent, the clergy who remember for Martin.
uses.paragraph: What we held instead was this. The test itself: everywhere, always, by all. The fathers, not one man - living old men for Cassian, collated doctors for Vincent, the clergy who remember for Martin. And the standing duty: one who preaches other than what was received is to be cut off, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. Cut off, not killed; bishops' sentence, not an emperor's sword.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The question names a struggle - cannot manage to believe - and asks what we would say.
uses.paragraph: The question names a struggle - cannot manage to believe - and asks what we would say. Here is what our record lets us answer. We did not keep an argument for the unbeliever. No one among us wrote down a proof of the resurrection for someone who doubts it. What we kept instead was this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. At Tours Martin was ten when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is our one formation story, and it is one man's. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that grace kindles the first desire, not the will itself. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. And we held it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all to be saved. So what we would say is not that you must manage it, but that the calling comes first and the willing follows. We never told anyone they had to argue themselves into faith. We kept the catechumen a long time, watched what grace did, and counted the beginning of every good thought as God's. Beyond that our record does not reach - we have no treatise for the doubter, only the witness that grace draws the unwilling.

uses.sentence: Our saint, alone in his cell, refused a purple-robed visitor who said *I am Christ* - and answered that he would believe only in one who came in the form in which he suffered, bearing the marks of his wounds.

uses.sentence: Martin could not easily be drawn from his monastery, so a citizen threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill.
uses.paragraph: The office fled and overtaken - that is the shape we lived. A man left the world for the stricter service of Christ, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, and a guard. Martin could not easily be drawn from his monastery, so a citizen threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. A bystander seized the psalter and read praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. Then the new bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.record_text: A monk is lured out of his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife is ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes and disgusting hair, and answered by a psalm opened at random.

use_note.means: Sulpitius reports that Martin was lured from his monastery by a pretext, escorted under guard, and made bishop of Tours though some bishops objected to his mean clothes.

uses.sentence: In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving.
uses.paragraph: The question you name as eternal fate was argued otherwise. Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it? Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour. Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.
uses.record_text: Holding on to the end - both the endurance a newcomer proves at the door and God's gift of keeping us in the good we have begun.

use_note.means: Perseverance meant holding on to the end, both the endurance a newcomer proves at the door and, in the grace argument, God's gift of keeping us in the good begun.
not_for: the later Reformed perseverance of the saints as eternal security
perseverance as sheer willpower

uses.sentence: The discipline for a fault is kept.
uses.paragraph: The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.
uses.record_text: The public discipline of our house. For a fault, a monk lies on the ground until the Abbot bids him rise, or is barred from prayer with the brethren. No priest is needed to restore him.

use_note.means: Penance meant the house's public discipline: lying on the ground until the Abbot bids rise, or barred from prayer, with no priest needed to restore the monk.

uses.sentence: That the fathers meant one stable thing across all three voices.
uses.paragraph: That the fathers meant one stable thing across all three voices. Vincent's collated doctors, Cassian's living Egyptian old men, and Martin's presbyters who remember - a scholar would ask whether those three senses of "the fathers" map onto each other the way our voice makes them seem to. That apostolic authority meant the same thing at Tours and at Marseilles. That Catholic, used by all three, carried one definition rather than three overlapping ones. The shared grammar we speak from is real - reception, antiquity, the office fled - but how much traffic it proves between the houses, a scholar would make us defend.
uses.record_text: The prior generations from whom everything legitimate among us is received and never invented. For Cassian, the Egyptian old men he sat with. For Vincent, the doctors whose collated writings form "a consentient council." For Martin, the presbyters who can say whether a tradition "had come down from antiquity."

use_note.means: The fathers meant the prior generations, as persons, from whom all legitimate teaching is received: living old men for Cassian, collated doctors for Vincent, remembering clergy for Martin.
not_for: a settled patristic canon of authors, or elders as a modern church office

uses.sentence: So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.record_text: For us tradition is what has been received from predecessors and must be passed on unchanged. Vincent's second criterion of truth after Scripture, "the Tradition of the Catholic Church." Pope Stephen's rule, "nothing but what has been handed down." Cassian's "traditions of the Elders" by which thoughts are judged. And the "steady tradition ... from antiquity" without which Martin will not honour a tomb.

use_note.means: Tradition meant what has been received and must be passed on unchanged, the ground on which Vincent's rule, Cassian's elders and Martin's refusal of a tomb are all judged.
not_for: a rival authority to Scripture in a confessional debate
custom and folkways, or conservatism

uses.sentence: Cassian never told how he came to believe.
uses.paragraph: No, never that phrase. What we kept for conversion is one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position, when its meaning is contested

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the whole program was received from Egypt's elders as the fathers' own.
uses.paragraph: The question of how what we kept connects to the earliest followers turns on a distinction we held as binding: received, not invented. What matters is not the age of a practice measured in years but whose it is - handed down from the fathers, or made up by us. Among the brethren at Marseilles the whole program was received from Egypt's elders as the fathers' own. The twelve psalms at evening and at night came, Cassian says, from the fathers of Egypt in the days when only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the offices should hold fifty or sixty psalms. The Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the founding story as Cassian carried it to us - not our own invention but Egypt's witness to itself. Egypt was our measure, in the south received as the fathers' own rule.

uses.sentence: It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.paragraph: And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. Our record does not speak of being born again. It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, mortification is the state of being dead to the world and its desires, figured as crucifixion. "As then one who is crucified no longer has the power of moving or turning his limbs in any direction as he pleases, so we also ought to affix our wishes and desires." It is read into the monk's very clothes. The girdle of dead skin "signifies that he bears about the mortification of those members in which are contained the seeds of lust."

use_note.means: Mortification meant being already dead to the world as a crucified man cannot move his limbs, the state every practice assumes, worn in the girdle and the tunic.
not_for: self-harm, self-hatred or flagellation

Salvian wrote of unburied dead and a petition for games. A scholar could check each sentence we speak against the page it cites, and the words would be there.

uses.sentence: The immediate goal of the whole life is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every practice is ranked by whether it serves that mark.
uses.paragraph: We read to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The purpose was not learning but living. The fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So the psalms keep the mill fed with what is good. The immediate goal of the whole life is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every practice is ranked by whether it serves that mark.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint's power was shown for the countryside people, the Gallic rustics who had scarcely heard the name of Christ.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the saint's power was shown for the countryside people, the Gallic rustics who had scarcely heard the name of Christ. He halted idols, burned temples, and built churches where they fell. A whole crowd was made catechumens by his one hand. And Martin himself stayed a catechumen for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak. After he raised a dead catechumen, the man told of a tribunal where two angels sent him back. Tours kept no teaching on who was saved; it kept the saint's labor for the unconverted, and one man's glimpse past death.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the unconverted countryside of Gaul. It was Martin's mission field. There he halted the veiled idols, burned temples, felled a sacred pine, and built churches where they fell.

uses.sentence: Beyond that edge, what the brethren at Tours actually sang, and at what hours, is not what our own record dwelt on.
uses.paragraph: I do not know what record you are naming. Nothing in the ground I am given to answer from this turn - and nothing else in the whole of our record as I hold it - speaks of any account of our worship obtained under torture. The brethren at Tours, as Sulpitius tells their life, kept the hours of prayer without a gap, and Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for those hours - the Spirit at the third, the Sacrifice at the sixth, the descent into hell at the ninth. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Beyond that edge, what the brethren at Tours actually sang, and at what hours, is not what our own record dwelt on. Of the island's own day - a rule kept, an office sung - nothing. And the three whole books and conferences on the body's discipline were cut from the one edition I can read by a nineteenth-century hand, not by our own silence.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature

uses.sentence: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, as Martin, many of Marmoutier's disciples and Honoratus passed from monk to bishop while keeping a monk's virtues inside the see.

uses.sentence: We said it as a thing already believed, not a thing we debated among ourselves.
uses.paragraph: Jesus is God. We said it as a thing already believed, not a thing we debated among ourselves. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So yes - we held there was no other way to say it.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives

uses.sentence: When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the newcomer as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door, then a year under the guest-Elder, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows, or the scorning at the door as hazing

uses.sentence: Giving up goods was only the first and easiest.
uses.paragraph: And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. Our record does not speak of being born again. It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world in three stages, of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act, or a heroic once-for-all rejection of society

uses.sentence: Yet bishops were the ones who ordained, judged doctrine, and held councils - and Martin would not sit with them after Trier.
uses.paragraph: Both houses held one thing the same. The office of bishop was not sought but seized - a man who left the world did not leave the Church, and the churches came for him. Martin was lured out by a lie and escorted under guard. Honoratus on the island fled, and the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and called it expulsion from the life as unworthy. Our own teaching made wanting the office a mark of vainglory and cold pride. Yet bishops were the ones who ordained, judged doctrine, and held councils - and Martin would not sit with them after Trier.
uses.record_text:
Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. The state, in this world's own view, has no right to judge the Church's own causes.
At Tours, the office is the thing fled. Bishops resist Martin's election (Vita IX). Some of Martin's slanderers, Sulpitius says, turned out to be bishops themselves, though very few (Vita XXVII). Before Maximus, Sulpitius writes, apostolic authority held its ground in Martin alone, while the priestly dignity around him bowed to the emperor's court (Vita XX). After the forced communion at Trier, Martin never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every assembly of bishops for the rest of his life (Dial. III.13). Sulpitius calls it a foul, unheard-of wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment on a matter belonging to the Church (Sacred History II.50).
At Marseilles, the office is both temptation and a defiance of the Pope. Cassian's Abbot Moses teaches that the devil can push a man to want holy orders under the pretext of doing good for many people (Conf. I.20). Vainglory brings a 'desire for the priesthood or diaconate' (Inst. XI.14). Archebius was 'expelled.' And, as the editor tells it, the Massilians held to their own views even against the authority of the Pope brought to bear on them.
At Lérins, the counter-current runs the other way. Vincent rules that an ancient General Council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness and ignorance of a few (Comm. ch. 3), and names 'the twofold authority of the Apostolic See' (ch. 32). Yet in the same voice, he holds that no rank exempts a lone dissenter: whether a teacher is holy and learned, a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr, a view held against the consent of all is only his own private fancy (ch. 28).
This tension never resolves evenly. Guarding antiquity by councils while fleeing synods, and producing bishops while distrusting the office, keeps this world from being reducible to a seminary that looked like a monastery. Over time it tips one way: the Lérins network becomes the very episcopate it once fled, and the argument over grace comes to be carried forward by a synodal commission - a shift that marks this world's own ending.

use_note.means: Bishops, synods and councils are honoured as guardians of the truth while Martin flees office and shuns synods after Trier, so authority is honoured and refused at once.

uses.sentence: But that is not the house answering to someone it failed; it is the saint's own judgment on himself.
uses.paragraph: And one elder is kept who confessed a power lessened. Martin took one communion he abhors, to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics, and afterward he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by it. But that is not the house answering to someone it failed; it is the saint's own judgment on himself.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus

uses.sentence: Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: First, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God does not will only some to be saved instead of all. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish, and to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. That is Abbot Chaeremon's own word, and we held it.
uses.record_text: For if He wills none of His little ones to perish, how can we, without grievous blasphemy, imagine He does not will all people's salvation? That He wills only some to be saved, instead of all people in general?

use_note.means: Chaeremon, in Cassian's Conference XIII, argues it would be grievous blasphemy to imagine God wills only some, rather than all, to be saved.

uses.sentence: Beyond that our record does not reach - we have no treatise for the doubter, only the witness that grace draws the unwilling.
uses.paragraph: The question names a struggle - cannot manage to believe - and asks what we would say. Here is what our record lets us answer. We did not keep an argument for the unbeliever. No one among us wrote down a proof of the resurrection for someone who doubts it. What we kept instead was this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. At Tours Martin was ten when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is our one formation story, and it is one man's. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that grace kindles the first desire, not the will itself. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. And we held it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all to be saved. So what we would say is not that you must manage it, but that the calling comes first and the willing follows. We never told anyone they had to argue themselves into faith. We kept the catechumen a long time, watched what grace did, and counted the beginning of every good thought as God's. Beyond that our record does not reach - we have no treatise for the doubter, only the witness that grace draws the unwilling.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.

uses.sentence: Martin kept silence, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds.
uses.paragraph: At Tours our one private word comes from Martin alone in his cell. The devil came dressed in purple with a crown of jewels and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. And he was the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate; Martin, still a catechumen and a soldier, cut his one cloak in two, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught the same: an elder broke his fast for strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: Where the record is thin - the island's own day, what Tours sang, the cut conferences on the body - we say so plainly [THIN GROUND: Lerins daily life] [THIN GROUND: chastity teaching].
uses.paragraph: We do not assert the events. We say what Cassian handed down, what Piamun told, what Gallus reports Martin said. We do not call the houses one institution or claim they knew of each other. We say they never wrote to each other, and we name the differences - power shown against power disowned, no traffic between them. Where the record is thin - the island's own day, what Tours sang, the cut conferences on the body - we say so plainly [THIN GROUND: Lerins daily life] [THIN GROUND: chastity teaching]. A scholar would respect that honesty, even as she questioned the frame that holds it all as one world. The frame is this build's wager. The honesty about what the frame does not hold is ours.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.sentence: Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen.
uses.paragraph: No, never that phrase. What we kept for conversion is one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.paragraph: At Tours the way in was different. Martin began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who turned to Christ against his parents' wish and stayed unbaptized for years. uses.sentence: When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives

uses.sentence: Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus reports that Martin refused to remove Brictio from the presbyterate when he was accused of crimes, lest he seem to avenge himself, saying Christ bore with Judas.

uses.sentence: Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the newcomer as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door, then a year under the guest-Elder, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows, or the scorning at the door as hazing

uses.sentence: That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
