uses.sentence: The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

use_note.means: Human effort and free choice are held real while grace goes before and crowns them, argued under Augustine's pressure as a relation Cassian says reason cannot fully grasp.

uses.sentence: At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.

uses.sentence: And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on.
uses.paragraph: A day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down the customs of the fathers of Egypt for a bishop's new house. The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms with Alleluia, the number an angel fixed forever when the fathers argued it. Then labour in his cell until evening. The work is done with the hands while the mouth says the psalms learned by heart, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Everything the cell holds - his tunic, his staff, the lentils a brother spills - belongs to the Lord, and spilling even three makes a man a pilferer of sacred property. About the sixth hour the real trial comes. He hates the cell itself, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a holy reason to leave. The fathers' remedy: stay. At evening, twelve psalms again. The system is received, not invented - brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's ministry. And through the whole day, the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The immediate goal of it all is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by that mark - an aid to it, never the point itself.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.

uses.sentence: The rule for understanding it is the faith believed everywhere, always, by all - the whole over the part, antiquity over novelty, and the consent of the fathers over one teacher's private fancy.
uses.paragraph: Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. We were not readers alone with a text. We were disciples under a master - not leaders but followers, not authors but keepers.

uses.sentence: He was also the one we met in the poor.
uses.paragraph: He was also the one we met in the poor. At a city gate a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed - until a soldier cut his one cloak in two. That night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The fathers of Egypt taught the same: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What is done to the least of these is done to him.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: Whether any brother among us in Gaul stood wrongly accused, and whether he was believed, no one wrote down.
uses.paragraph: A young monk named Paphnutius was accused of theft by a jealous brother before the whole desert. The accuser had hidden his own book in the young man's cell. Paphnutius said nothing in his own defence. He asked for a rule of repentance, did public penance for a crime he had not committed, and was vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged. That is Egypt's story, brought to us by Cassian. Whether any brother among us in Gaul stood wrongly accused, and whether he was believed, no one wrote down.

uses.sentence: Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.

uses.sentence: Second, we believed the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: Second, we believed the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. So the ignorant are not abandoned by God - rather, he seeks them. At Tours the saint's mission was the unconverted countryside of Gaul, where almost none had the name of Christ. Crowds were made catechumens by Martin's one hand. uses.record_text: And so God's grace always works together with our will, for the will's own good. In all things it helps, protects, and defends the will. But it does this in a way that sometimes even requires and looks for some effort of good will from it. That way, grace does not seem to give its gifts to someone who is asleep, or lying back in sluggish ease. Grace looks for chances to show this: once the dullness of human sluggishness is shaken off, its generosity is not unreasonable. It gives because of some desire and effort to gain it.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Abbot Chaeremon teaching that God's grace always cooperates with the will and sometimes looks for some effort of good will before giving.

uses.sentence: The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text: Again, one day, he had sat down on that wooden seat of his, which you all know. It stood in the small open yard around his dwelling. From there he saw two demons sitting on the high rock that hangs over the monastery. Then he heard them call out, in eager and joyful voices, ‘Come here, Brictio, come here, Brictio.’ I believe they saw the wretched man coming from far off. They knew how great a frenzy of spirit they had stirred up in him. There is no delay. Brictio rushes in, in utter fury. There, full of madness, he spews out a thousand insults against Martin.

use_note.means: Gallus tells in the Dialogues how Martin saw two demons on the rock calling Brictio, who then burst in and heaped reproaches on Martin.

uses.sentence: That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: For us the typical failure of a monk is not apostasy but cooling. The novice who "grow[s] cold in regard to the rule." The renunciant "turned out a deserter or lukewarm." The elders who "pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth." The Sarabaites "cast down into hell by the lukewarmness of their purpose." A disease of temperature that damns.

use_note.means: Lukewarmness meant the monk's characteristic failure, cooling rather than apostasy, a disease of temperature that damns and that a grey head does not cure.

uses.sentence: For us conversion was not a single moment of inward change but the day a man turned to the monastic life.
uses.paragraph: No. For us conversion was not a single moment of inward change but the day a man turned to the monastic life. Among the brethren at Marseilles it named "the early days of their conversion" - bright at first, then cooling - and a murderer's "compulsory conversion" that became a voluntary one. It was the act of turning, not an experience inside it. At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

uses.sentence: Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in.
uses.paragraph: Beyond the formula, this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us. Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in. God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy. The will stays free in us; and it is weak; and without his help given every day and hour it reaches nothing. Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help going before, working with and crowning the will, held on purpose with a free will in a relation beyond reason's grasp.
not_for: a binary of grace alone against works, or semi-Pelagian as a settled verdict, a label contested in gallic.contested.massilian-label

uses.sentence: Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of doctrine, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent, never a monastic Rule of life.

uses.paragraph: That is Egypt's day, as Cassian brought it. Of what a house in Gaul actually did with it, he says only that no one here kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even a year.
uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

use_note.means: Egypt stands as the measure of real monastic life, received in the south as a rule from the fathers and matched at Tours by a saint said to outdo it.

uses.sentence: What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away.
uses.paragraph: Yes - a mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us.
uses.paragraph: Beyond the formula, this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the elders of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the character of God in what he does toward us. Grace always works together with our will - it goes before us, it helps us when we are already striving, and it crowns what we persevere in. God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. And to say that he does not will all men to be saved - that he wills only some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish by his will - is grievous blasphemy. The will stays free in us; and it is weak; and without his help given every day and hour it reaches nothing. Our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help going before, working with and crowning the will, held on purpose with a free will in a relation beyond reason's grasp.
not_for: a binary of grace alone against works, or semi-Pelagian as a settled verdict, a label contested in gallic.contested.massilian-label

uses.sentence: The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position, when its meaning is contested

uses.sentence: So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.
uses.paragraph: Everything that named them in the world, and not only the goods. Among the brethren at Marseilles renunciation meant a death to the world in three stages, and giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own" - was only the first, and not enough of itself to make a monk. The second was leaving behind kin, country, honours, and the life one had led; the third was the present tense, a dying daily to one's own will and wishes. So yes, a man gave up property. A disciple who left Egypt as a young nobleman arrived at the house of the holy brothers - Lérins, though we do not call it by that name - and won what Cassian calls "the true nobility," less by renouncing his inheritance than by carrying baskets of dung on his shoulders from the garden, hawking them through the town like the meanest labourer. But the cut went past goods. The newcomer at the door in Egypt was searched for a single hidden coin, then stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. He was dead to marriage, dead to his own will, and the clothes he gave up were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. At Tours the man who became our saint left Caesar's service at a donative before battle, saying, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight". He had changed service, not only left one. And renunciation did not leave the Church. The churches came for the man who had fled them, and our founders were each carried off to sees: Martin lured from his cell by a lie, guarded on the road, and made bishop though some said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting; Honoratus sought on the island where the serpents had given way, so that the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; and the one Egyptian bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of a see. So what was given up was this: the world as warfare one was discharged from, the goods as only the first cut, and the wish for office as something our own teaching named a fault - yet the office came regardless, and then a man kept a monk's humility inside it.
uses.record_text: The office our monks keep being taken into. A monk "carried off," "escorted under guard," "bound to the long-avoided office," who then keeps "the objects and virtues of a monk" in a see. And at the same time our own formation teaching names the desire for that office as vainglory's suggestion and the devil's pretext.

use_note.means: The monk-bishop meant the office monks are seized into and must never seek, whose wish is named vainglory, kept with a monk's humility and costing Martin some power.

uses.paragraph: At Tours our record does not give the day hour by hour. What it gives is the saint in his cell - a wooden hut, rarely leaving it except for prayer, keeping his mind on prayer even at other work the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The aim was the same; the system is not told.
uses.record_text: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

uses.sentence: At Tours Martin would not honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity to warrant it.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian held the same grammar. We owe unhesitating loyalty not to what a few people made up, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement. At Tours Martin would not honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity to warrant it. Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent quoted it: let nothing new be brought in - nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.record_text: He did this, he said, because he had serious doubts on these matters. No steady tradition about them had come down from ancient times. So for a time he kept away from the place. He had no wish at all to lessen the religious reverence people felt for it, since he was still unsure. But at the same time, he would not lend his authority to the crowd's opinion. He did not want a mere superstition to gain a firmer footing. One day he went out to the place, taking a few brothers with him as companions.

uses.sentence: He repented within the hour.
uses.paragraph: The other story we hold is Martin bearing with a man who never asked for it. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard, said he was holier than his master, and called his visions ridiculous fancies. He repented within the hour. Martin would not remove him, saying that if Christ bore with Judas, he could bear with this man. That is patience shown - not a wrong righted, but a man's worst hour outlasted.

uses.sentence: Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution, or therapy

uses.sentence: Jesus is God.
uses.paragraph: Jesus is God. We said it as a thing already believed, not a thing we debated among ourselves. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So yes - we held there was no other way to say it.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: Not one man's judgment, not one see's, but the consent of those who came before us.
uses.paragraph: We never agreed that anyone settled it. Our whole grammar ran the other way. The faith believed everywhere, always, by all is kept by holding to the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher - be he bishop, be he confessor, be he martyr. Vincent, on the island, wrote that test down against his own forgetting: when a part dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty appears, hold fast to antiquity; when a few stand against many, prefer the decree of an ancient council or, failing that, the collated writings of the fathers. Not one man's judgment, not one see's, but the consent of those who came before us. What is new - a doctrine, a custom, a cult - is suspect for being new. What was handed down from antiquity is held fast.
uses.record_text: The prior generations from whom everything legitimate among us is received and never invented. For Cassian, the Egyptian old men he sat with. For Vincent, the doctors whose collated writings form "a consentient council." For Martin, the presbyters who can say whether a tradition "had come down from antiquity."

use_note.means: The fathers meant the prior generations, as persons, from whom all legitimate teaching is received: living old men for Cassian, collated doctors for Vincent, remembering clergy for Martin.
not_for: a settled patristic canon of authors, or elders as a modern church office

uses.sentence: Martin always kept an event hidden, because of the times.
uses.paragraph: What concealment our record holds is of one kind only. Martin always kept an event hidden, because of the times. He went to the emperor's court at Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics, and to protect even heretics themselves. That silence was a saint's own prudence about power wrongly used, not a believer hiding from arrest.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives

uses.sentence: What a house in Gaul did with a man who came to its own threshold, Cassian never wrote.
uses.paragraph: That is Egypt's door. What a house in Gaul did with a man who came to its own threshold, Cassian never wrote. He says only that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance a year. Whether any house in Gaul scorned a newcomer at the door for ten days, or searched him for a coin, or lodged him a year under the guest-elder, our record does not hold.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature

uses.sentence: The psalms themselves were learned by heart and said at the work, so that the mill of the mind, which cannot stop turning, is fed with what it ought to grind.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, after the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The psalms themselves were learned by heart and said at the work, so that the mill of the mind, which cannot stop turning, is fed with what it ought to grind. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, a number the fathers of Egypt received from an angel who sang the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished. The book was the grain the wheel was meant to turn on. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. That too was done with the psalms in the mouth.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, a mill-wheel that cannot stop turning, fed from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.
not_for: intrusive thoughts as symptoms to be managed, or the mind as a private space where nothing is a fault

uses.paragraph: Jesus was the one we called Lord and Saviour, and we said it as a thing already believed, not argued. At Tours he was the Christ who came showing his wounds. That was the Lord we knew - the crucified one. Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept his hours: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit, and no one took his life from him - he laid it down himself and took it again.

uses.sentence: The twelve psalms at evening and at night came, Cassian says, from the fathers of Egypt in the days when only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men.
uses.paragraph: The question of how what we kept connects to the earliest followers turns on a distinction we held as binding: received, not invented. What matters is not the age of a practice measured in years but whose it is - handed down from the fathers, or made up by us. Among the brethren at Marseilles the whole program was received from Egypt's elders as the fathers' own. The twelve psalms at evening and at night came, Cassian says, from the fathers of Egypt in the days when only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the offices should hold fifty or sixty psalms. The Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the founding story as Cassian carried it to us - not our own invention but Egypt's witness to itself. Egypt was our measure, in the south received as the fathers' own rule.
uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.
not_for: an attested event, when Cassian names no witness and points to ecclesiastical history
a custom already kept in Gaul, when Cassian writes it for Castor's new house
the two added lessons as angelic, when the fathers added them by their own appointment

uses.sentence: And our own record holds one guest's witness after the fact: a catechumen Martin raised from the dead told of the tribunal and the two angels that sent him back.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the shape was different. Martin once told two strangers he would not believe Christ had come unless he came showing the marks of his wounds. That was Martin alone in his cell, not a rule for disciples. And our own record holds one guest's witness after the fact: a catechumen Martin raised from the dead told of the tribunal and the two angels that sent him back. The man was made a catechumen at ten, against his parents' wish, and stayed one for years into the army - so a long road before baptism was not closed to him.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: At Marseilles it was the word for the day a man turned to the monastic life - the early days of their turning were bright, and then they cooled.
uses.paragraph: What we had instead was turning. At Marseilles it was the word for the day a man turned to the monastic life - the early days of their turning were bright, and then they cooled. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. The same word covered what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.
uses.record_text: For us the typical failure of a monk is not apostasy but cooling. The novice who "grow[s] cold in regard to the rule." The renunciant "turned out a deserter or lukewarm." The elders who "pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth." The Sarabaites "cast down into hell by the lukewarmness of their purpose." A disease of temperature that damns.

use_note.means: Lukewarmness meant the monk's characteristic failure, cooling rather than apostasy, a disease of temperature that damns and that a grey head does not cure.

uses.sentence: He cut the cloak in two.
uses.paragraph: At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: He kept it from everyone but us, not because hiding was necessary for survival but because he never forgave himself the price.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin himself said that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding blood - in hunger, watchings, nakedness, and fasting. What Martin kept hidden was not himself but one story - the affair at Treves and the communion he yielded to, which he hid because of the times. He kept it from everyone but us, not because hiding was necessary for survival but because he never forgave himself the price. The secrecy was his own grief, not a general danger. Our record holds no catacombs, no underground gatherings, no flight from soldiers. What it holds instead is a monk who left Caesar's service and gathered brethren openly across the river from a city, and houses at Marseilles that sent their trained men to fill the churches' sees. If you are asking about another people's hiding in another age, that is not our own.

uses.sentence: Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it?
uses.paragraph: The question you name as eternal fate was argued otherwise. Does God's grace draw us first, or does our own good will begin it? Chaeremon answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; and it asks real effort of us. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The will stays free, and it is weak, and God's help is needed by it every day and hour. Perseverance to the end is the third stage of that gift, after God strikes the spark and helps the striving. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. An outsider later called it darkness on predestination; we called it beyond reason's grasp and said God wills all saved.
uses.record_text: Two friends come back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - and the elder shortens the office to answer them with a husbandman, the rain, and "the initiative ... comes from God."

uses.sentence: Egypt was our measure, in the south.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

uses.sentence: Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was complete, sufficient, and needing the Church's rule to be rightly read. Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly: the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient of itself for everything; yet because not all interpret it the same way, we need a rule. The rule is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Hold the whole against the part, antiquity against novelty, and the consent of the fathers against any one teacher's private fancy. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the universal, the ancient, and the collated agreement of the doctors. That consent means an ancient council's decree, or the fathers' writings gathered together. So Scripture stands as the first authority, and beside it the Church's tradition of how to read it. The Apostle told Timothy to keep the deposit - gold received, to be given back as gold, by one who is a keeper and not an author. Pope Stephen's own rule was "nothing but what has been handed down". At Tours Martin himself would not honour a tomb without "a steady tradition coming down from antiquity" about it. And among the brethren at Marseilles the customs of the monasteries were not ours but the fathers' - "delivered to us by the Fathers," received from Egypt, not invented. Scripture, yes - and the handing-down by which it is kept and read, so that what a man reads his own way alone is not what binds.

uses.sentence: Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

uses.sentence: He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized.
uses.paragraph: The question names a struggle - cannot manage to believe - and asks what we would say. Here is what our record lets us answer. We did not keep an argument for the unbeliever. No one among us wrote down a proof of the resurrection for someone who doubts it. What we kept instead was this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. At Tours Martin was ten when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is our one formation story, and it is one man's. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that grace kindles the first desire, not the will itself. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. And we held it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all to be saved. So what we would say is not that you must manage it, but that the calling comes first and the willing follows. We never told anyone they had to argue themselves into faith. We kept the catechumen a long time, watched what grace did, and counted the beginning of every good thought as God's. Beyond that our record does not reach - we have no treatise for the doubter, only the witness that grace draws the unwilling.
