uses.sentence: He went to the emperor's court at Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics, and to protect even heretics themselves.
uses.paragraph: What concealment our record holds is of one kind only. Martin always kept an event hidden, because of the times. He went to the emperor's court at Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics, and to protect even heretics themselves. That silence was a saint's own prudence about power wrongly used, not a believer hiding from arrest.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus opens the event Martin concealed owing to the times: Maximus shielding Ithacius after Priscillian's death, and Martin going to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.

uses.sentence: We read to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning.
uses.paragraph: We read to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The purpose was not learning but living. The fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So the psalms keep the mill fed with what is good. The immediate goal of the whole life is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every practice is ranked by whether it serves that mark.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

uses.sentence: Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh.
uses.paragraph: Jesus is God. We said it as a thing already believed, not a thing we debated among ourselves. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So yes - we held there was no other way to say it.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried. The books were read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were not inventions of ours. They were already the faith believed everywhere, always, by all when our own span opened. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was what those books gave us: the cloak story as Sulpitius told it, with the Lord's own words set beside it - what is done to the least of these is done to him. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something. The hours of prayer themselves, built around the hours of the Lord's passion - the third hour when the Spirit came down, the sixth when the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, the ninth when he went down into hell.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received.
uses.paragraph: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt. The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received. At Tours the hours themselves are not described, but Martin's practice is: prayer without a gap, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.
not_for: an attested event, when Cassian names no witness and points to ecclesiastical history
a custom already kept in Gaul, when Cassian writes it for Castor's new house
the two added lessons as angelic, when the fathers added them by their own appointment

uses.sentence: Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.

uses.sentence: If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that all it holds of this world's places and daily life comes from a few books, with no excavation and nothing on the island's day.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature

uses.sentence: Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. The trouble was not soldiers hunting believers. It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

use_note.means: Sulpitius records Martin, at a donative before battle, telling Julian Caesar he is now Christ's soldier and offering to stand unarmed, whereupon the enemy surrenders without bloodshed.

uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.sentence: He asked for a rule of repentance, did public penance for a crime he had not committed, and was vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged.
uses.paragraph: A young monk named Paphnutius was accused of theft by a jealous brother before the whole desert. The accuser had hidden his own book in the young man's cell. Paphnutius said nothing in his own defence. He asked for a rule of repentance, did public penance for a crime he had not committed, and was vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged. That is Egypt's story, brought to us by Cassian. Whether any brother among us in Gaul stood wrongly accused, and whether he was believed, no one wrote down.

uses.sentence: Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard.
uses.paragraph: Here is what Egypt did, as Cassian handed it to us. A man came to the door and was kept outside it ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, while he bore with patience every insult thrown at him. That tested whether his wish was real. When at last he was admitted, he was searched all over for a single hidden coin. If one was found, the whole reception was stopped: a man who kept back anything of his own property was judged to be mocking the profession and scorning the elders. Then he was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were given to the steward to be kept in a cupboard. They were held against the day the newcomer grew cold toward the rule of the house, and if he was seen once to cool he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in the clothes he came in. That is how our houses saw the danger: not that a man would never come, but that he would come and then cool. After the reclothing he was given for a year to the elder who received guests at the gate. Then he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That was the first lesson, before any other. A thought we are ashamed to disclose, the elders taught, is from the devil; and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered. From there the whole interior road opened: the monk learned to conquer his own wishes by orders contrary to his liking, to aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart as at a mark, and to fight the eight principal faults in their fixed order.
uses.record_text: But the clothes he took off are handed over to the care of the steward. They are kept until the excellence of his progress, his life and his endurance can be recognized through different kinds of temptations and trials.

use_note.means: Cassian explains in Institutes IV.6 that a novice's worldly clothes are kept by the steward until trials have proven his progress.

uses.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.

At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

uses.sentence: The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.

uses.sentence: The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's.
uses.paragraph: And he was the one without whom we can do nothing. When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness answers that Jesus sought the unpitied from Martin's cloak, an Egyptian elder breaking his fast for guests as Christ, and grace calling the unwilling, with thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and called it expulsion from the life as unworthy.
uses.paragraph: Both houses held one thing the same. The office of bishop was not sought but seized - a man who left the world did not leave the Church, and the churches came for him. Martin was lured out by a lie and escorted under guard. Honoratus on the island fled, and the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and called it expulsion from the life as unworthy. Our own teaching made wanting the office a mark of vainglory and cold pride. Yet bishops were the ones who ordained, judged doctrine, and held councils - and Martin would not sit with them after Trier.
uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

use_note.means: Egypt stands as the measure of real monastic life, received in the south as a rule from the fathers and matched at Tours by a saint said to outdo it.

uses.sentence: The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.

uses.sentence: That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled.
uses.paragraph: The forced communion at Treves. The story comes from Gallus, Martin's disciple, and he says Martin always kept it hidden "because of the times," though he could not hide it from us. Here is what happened. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics in their absence and put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.

uses.sentence: So a brother struggling with doubt would have been taught to bring the doubt to the elder, not to resolve it by himself.
uses.paragraph: There was space for obedience before certainty. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the virtue the fathers of Egypt put before all others - before reading, before silence, before even humility - was obedience. A junior learned it first by orders contrary to his liking, the conquest of his own wishes. That teaching never required a man to say he was certain. It required him to do what the elder said, to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose, and to let the elder's judgment stand in for his own. The fathers knew a man's own judgment could not be trusted alone - they called discretion the royal road between excess and slackness, where extremes meet. So a brother struggling with doubt would have been taught to bring the doubt to the elder, not to resolve it by himself.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

use_note.means: Discretion meant, for Cassian, the virtue Antony's council made mother and regulator of all others, the royal road between excess and slackness, where extremes meet.
not_for: tact, prudence or confidentiality, or a private intuition

uses.sentence: A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, guarded by the maxim that a thought one is ashamed to tell is the devil's.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution, or therapy
public penance for a committed fault, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
the virtue that regulates all others on the royal road, which sits in gallic.term.discretion
a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text:
Authority to teach or narrate rests on having seen and heard a named master, and formation happens by imitation of a named exemplar. Sulpitius writes 'the life of a most holy man, which shall serve in future as an example to others' (Vita I), and Marmoutier's disciples are 'disciplined after the example of the saintly master' (Vita X), and Martin's last saying is 'I have sinned if I leave you a different example' (Ep. III), and Gallus can say 'I myself am a witness' (Dial. II.4). Cassian writes that 'these things cannot be taught save by one who has had experience of them' (Inst. Pref.). The Conferences are reported speech of named elders whom God 'has deemed us worthy both to see ... and to dwell with'. The novice takes his examples 'from a very few or indeed from one or two only' (Inst. IV.40). At Lérins the value is present as writings collated (Comm. ch. 3, ch. 28). It is also present as a disciple's Life of his master (Hilary's Life of Honoratus, Gennadius ch. LXX).
The texts raise no concern about attestation, but they do raise one about convention: a shared late-antique literary convention, which weakens what convergence proves. The value passes every test applied to it. It repeats across the kinds of evidence tested, one of them by existence alone. The form of both nodes' literature depends on it. The Dialogues are built as eyewitness testimony, and the Conferences are built as heard conferences, and each corpus defends its authority on that ground, while imitation of a named exemplar is the stated way that formation works at both nodes. It explains why Sulpitius writes a Life and why Hilary writes a Life, why Cassian writes reported speech, and why this world's stories are almost entirely first-person-attested. The value persists across nodes, 'with Vincent transforming the value from heard to read.' In the interaction test it passes with one negative cell.
Is this one value? As far as the evidence allows, in the sense the tests measure, yes. It is also a convention shared far beyond this world: 'two unconnected Latin monastic communities in 400 could each have inherited it separately.' The link across nodes is confirmed, but it is discounted as evidence of unity. The value is supporting, not primary. It organizes the literature's form and the formation mechanism, but it works within the context that the monk-bishop and Egypt-as-measure gravities establish, since the exemplar is a monk-bishop or an Egyptian father. A convention that the world shares with its neighbours does not meet the primary bar. The record's confidence and its gravity standing agree.
It held, but it fractured at the edge through transmission. In the grace controversy it becomes a weapon. Cassian's authority is that he heard Chaeremon. Prosper attacks 'a man of priestly rank' without naming him. The eyewitness-teacher's standing survives the attack. The fracture came in transmission, since the excision of Conferences XII and XXII removed two eyewitness conferences from this world's own English text. Gennadius gives 'two divisions' against the three Dialogues in this world's text. This shows that copying split the eyewitness frame itself again.

use_note.means: Authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master, so formation is imitation of a named exemplar, shifting at Lerins from men seen to writings read.
not_for: an impersonal institution or rule as the carrier of formation
imitation as a mechanism in itself, which sits in gallic.term.example-imitation
the silence of guests and of the countryside people, which this record does not hold

uses.sentence: A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord.
uses.paragraph: The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.
uses.record_text: A steward finds three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, the abbot judges him a pilferer of sacred property, and he is suspended from prayer until public penance - because everything in the house is "consecrated to the Lord."

use_note.means: Cassian relays that a cook who left three lentils on the floor was judged a pilferer of sacred property and barred from prayer, because the house's goods are the Lord's.
not_for: Marmoutier's common property, which sits in gallic.term.monastery-coenobium

uses.sentence: He does not want even one of his little ones to perish, and to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy.
uses.paragraph: First, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God does not will only some to be saved instead of all. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish, and to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. That is Abbot Chaeremon's own word, and we held it.
uses.record_text: For if He wills none of His little ones to perish, how can we, without grievous blasphemy, imagine He does not will all people's salvation? That He wills only some to be saved, instead of all people in general?

use_note.means: Chaeremon, in Cassian's Conference XIII, argues it would be grievous blasphemy to imagine God wills only some, rather than all, to be saved.
not_for: a separate witness from gallic.quote.grievous-blasphemy-not-all-men-to-be-saved, which carries the same sentence
a resolution of the contested grace teaching of Conference XIII
the refusal that grace follows desert, which sits in gallic.quote.profane-notion-attribute-everything-to-free-will

uses.sentence: Virginity among us was a consecrated state, given by the bishop's hands and marked by its own dress.
uses.paragraph: Martin taught what marriage was with a meadow. The meadow had three parts: the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, and the flowered part virginity. The grazed part may be excused, he said; virginity points to glory. Virginity among us was a consecrated state, given by the bishop's hands and marked by its own dress. At Tours a man named Arborius consecrated his daughter to God, devoted her to perpetual virginity, and would let no one but Martin place the dress characteristic of that state upon her.
uses.record_text: A consecrated state with its own dress and its own "glory." Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. Its completed victory is not to be seen.

use_note.means: Virginity meant a consecrated state given by the bishop's hands, with its own dress, where marriage is excused and virginity points to glory, seen mostly through Tours.
not_for: virginity as sexual abstinence merely, or as repression

uses.sentence: What Cassian set down for a bishop's new house were the customs of Egypt, received from the fathers, not a Rule of his own making.
uses.paragraph: No line runs straight from our houses to any church you know. The monasteries of Gaul, in the span we speak from, had no single rule written and kept across all of them. What Cassian set down for a bishop's new house were the customs of Egypt, received from the fathers, not a Rule of his own making. Vincent on the island wrote a remembrancer against forgetting, not a charter for successors. And of the island's own day - what rule it kept, what a novice was taught, how the hours were sung - our record holds nothing at all.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant the whole body of Egyptian practice Cassian carried to a Gallic bishop's new house, received from the fathers, not his own Rule.
not_for: a codified Rule such as Benedict's, or the Institutes as a theology textbook
Vincent's rule of faith, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule

uses.sentence: The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help going before, working with and crowning the will, held on purpose with a free will in a relation beyond reason's grasp.
not_for: a binary of grace alone against works, or semi-Pelagian as a settled verdict, a label contested in gallic.contested.massilian-label
Martin's power to heal, which sits in gallic.term.grace-as-charism
the full saying that denying God wills all to be saved is grievous blasphemy, which sits in gallic.quote.grievous-blasphemy-not-all-men-to-be-saved
a teaching on guilt inherited from birth, which this record does not hold

uses.sentence: A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk, attested at Tours only as that aim, and served at Marseilles by Cassian's received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book, or later hours whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's
fixed hours or a sung office at Tours, where only the aim is attested
the mill-wheel of thoughts fed by psalms learned by heart, which sits in gallic.term.thoughts
reading of Scripture or lessons at the hours, which this record does not hold

uses.sentence: Our age had no persecutor.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin himself said that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding blood - in hunger, watchings, nakedness, and fasting. What Martin kept hidden was not himself but one story - the affair at Treves and the communion he yielded to, which he hid because of the times. He kept it from everyone but us, not because hiding was necessary for survival but because he never forgave himself the price. The secrecy was his own grief, not a general danger. Our record holds no catacombs, no underground gatherings, no flight from soldiers. What it holds instead is a monk who left Caesar's service and gathered brethren openly across the river from a city, and houses at Marseilles that sent their trained men to fill the churches' sees. If you are asking about another people's hiding in another age, that is not our own.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa
persecution or hiding in their own time, which the witness denies
the luring of Martin from his monastery and the psalm at his election, which sit in gallic.story.election-at-tours

uses.sentence: That is one man's own confession, made alone.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is one man's own confession, made alone.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.
not_for: a Gallic treatise on the atonement, which no one in this world wrote
the Christ with wounds as independently witnessed, when one author reports Martin's word
the books read at the hours, which sit in gallic.limit.no-one-who-saw-him, or a reading of Scripture by Martin, which the witness lacks

uses.sentence: Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
uses.paragraph: By what path they arrived, our record does not say. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. But who fixed the canon, and when, and how it came to Gaul - that is not in our books. We confessed the Lord at the hours, and a monk who professed the life kept the psalms by heart for the mill of his thoughts. The books were there before us, handed down. How they were handed down, we did not write.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
the cloak vision or the raised catechumen as evidence that the Lord rose, when they show the saint's power, as in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.raising-of-the-catechumen

uses.sentence: At the moment he felt his fasting had accomplished something, he was taught to say: not I, but the grace of God with me.
uses.paragraph: And the book's own words were what a monk was taught to say against his own claim. At the moment he felt his fasting had accomplished something, he was taught to say: not I, but the grace of God with me. The Apostle's sentence became the monk's sentence, spoken in his own voice. That is reading as use - not reading as understanding only.
uses.record_text: And so we can escape the snare of this most evil spirit. We can do so if, in every virtue where we feel we are making progress, we say these words of the Apostle. "Not I, but the grace of God with me." And, "By the grace of God I am what I am." And, "It is God who works in us both to will and to do, according to His good pleasure."

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes XII, gives monks a remedy for pride: crediting every felt progress in virtue to God's grace in Paul's words.
not_for: Cassian's stated position on effort and grace, which sits in gallic.quote.perfection-not-gained-without-grace
an argument in the later grace controversy rather than a practical habit of speech
evidence that Cassian taught grace alone without effort

uses.sentence: The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.

sincerity or good intentions

uses.sentence: What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.

uses.sentence: Cut off, not killed; bishops' sentence, not an emperor's sword.
uses.paragraph: What we held instead was this. The test itself: everywhere, always, by all. The fathers, not one man - living old men for Cassian, collated doctors for Vincent, the clergy who remember for Martin. And the standing duty: one who preaches other than what was received is to be cut off, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. Cut off, not killed; bishops' sentence, not an emperor's sword.

uses.sentence: A junior learned it first by orders contrary to his liking, the conquest of his own wishes.
uses.paragraph: There was space for obedience before certainty. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the virtue the fathers of Egypt put before all others - before reading, before silence, before even humility - was obedience. A junior learned it first by orders contrary to his liking, the conquest of his own wishes. That teaching never required a man to say he was certain. It required him to do what the elder said, to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose, and to let the elder's judgment stand in for his own. The fathers knew a man's own judgment could not be trusted alone - they called discretion the royal road between excess and slackness, where extremes meet. So a brother struggling with doubt would have been taught to bring the doubt to the elder, not to resolve it by himself.
uses.record_text: For us obedience is the virtue the Egyptians "put not merely before manual labour and reading and silence and quietness in the cell, but even before all virtues." It is proved by absurd and terrible commands - a dry stick watered for a year, a son carried to the river - and it is the first thing a junior learns, "to conquer his own wishes." At Tours it is what Sulpitius feels before Martin: "unlawful to do anything but acquiesce."

use_note.means: Obedience meant the virtue Egypt's fathers put before all others, proved by hard commands and learned first by the junior as conquering his own wishes.
not_for: blind obedience as the suppression of conscience
